posts.title: Acquired Neurodivergence and workplace: Acquired Neurodivergence & Neurodivergence In The Workplace
posts.text:
Acquired Neurodivergence & Neurodivergence In The Workplace

Qualified Forensic Scientist
Independent Academic in the field of critical theory, mental health, and neuroqueer theory
Multiply published author
Consultant, mentor, and advocate
Co-founder of Autistic Substance Use Network (ASUN)
Practitioner Member of Addiction Professionals
Professional Member of International Society of Substance Use Professionals (ISSUP)

Why This Conversation Matters
Neurodivergent people are at greater risk of mental health challenges—but the story is more nuanced than pathology. Through the neurodiversity paradigm we can understand that neurodivergence is not just limited to Autism & ADHD. It can also be acquired through trauma and mistreatment.
For public facing professionals, and employers, it is important to understand the full scope of neurodivergence and how it may impact on us.

Note On Language
For example, Autistic person, rather than “person with autism”.
The neurodivergent community widely feels that such language only adds to the stigma around their lives.

What does neurodiversity really mean?
If there are 8 billion people in the world, then there are 8 billion unique brains.
Many can perform neuronormative standards comfortably, and are considered “neurotypical”.
A significant portion find this difficult, and by means of their cognition, behaviour, and experience, are identified as neurodivergent; They diverge from neuronormative standards.
A person can be born neurodivergent (innate neurodivergence) or acquire it later in life (acquired neurodivergence).

posts.title: Acquired Neurodivergence and workplace: Trauma and Acquired Neurodivergence
posts.text:
Trauma and Acquired Neurodivergence
Trauma doesn't have to be a singular event – it can be cumulative.
Trauma can predispose our brain to mental health challenges.
Trauma is not necessarily something that is life threatening or dangerous. Many things can traumatise us and make us feel unsafe in the world.
This has been framed as illness overtime, but another way of considering this altering of our brain is as acquired neurodivergence.

Examples Of Acquired Neurodivergence
Obsessive Compulsive Disorder
Bipolar
Schizophrenia
Other psychotic conditions and voice hearing
Personality Disorders
Traumatic Brain Injury
Epilepsy
This non-exhaustive list are all neurodivergence we can acquire over the course of our lives.

Why Frame It As Neurodivergence?
Normative attitudes in society have resulted in the dehumanisation of minds that exist outside of cultural standards of “normal”
Neuronormativity has resulted in the belief that we must all adhere to one style of thought, feeling, and expression
Neurodivergence allows us to move away from the stigma of mental illness and towards a more inclusive and empowering approach to supporting people in distress

Why Is This Significant To Autistic & ADHD People?

posts.title: Acquired Neurodivergence and workplace: Autistic & ADHD People Are More Likely To Acquire Further Neurodivergence
posts.text:
Autistic & ADHD People Are More Likely To Acquire Further Neurodivergence
Autistic people are significantly more likely to receive a co-occurring psychiatric diagnosis (acquired neurodivergence) (Lai et al. , 2019)
As many os 89% of ADHD people receive a psychiatric diagnosis (Sobanski, 2006)
Lai, M. C. , Kassee, C. , Besney, R. , Bonato, S. , Hull, L. , Mandy, W. , ... & Ameis, S. H. (2019). Prevalence of co-occurring mental health diagnoses in the autism population: a systematic review and meta-analysis. The Lancet Psychiatry, 6(10), 819-829.
Sobanski, E. (2006). Psychiatric comorbidity in adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). European archives of psychiatry and clinical neuroscience, 256(Suppl 1), i26-i31.

Diagnostic Overshadowing
Autistic and ADHD individuals commonly report that their acquired neurodivergence and related distress is misattributed to their Autism or ADHD despite not being a part of diagnostic criteria
Conversely, many people are diagnosed with psychiatric conditions and then later have these rediagnosed as Autism and/or ADHD
This suggests a clinical ambiguity in diagnostic practices and potential barriers to support for Autistic and ADHD people who are struggling as a result of acquired neurodivergence.

posts.title: Acquired Neurodivergence and workplace: Predisposition To Acquired Neurodivergence
posts.text:
Predisposition To Acquired Neurodivergence
Many innately neurodivergent people describe the world as not being designed for them
They find many aspects of the environments around them challenging or even harmful
This creates an increased potential for Autistic and ADHD people to acquire further neurodivergence and experience the distress associated with it

Neurodivergence In The Workplace

The Impact Of Environment
Dr. Luke Beardon proposed the following:
Autism + Environment = Outcome
Autism, however, could be substituted for any kind of neurodivergence
Neurodivergence can not be undone, but we can alter the environment to better accommodate it
When the environment is more accommodating, we experience better outcomes
Unemployment or loss of employment is a significant issue for neurodivergent people largely because workplace environments do not appropriately support their needs

The Double Empathy Problem
The Double Empathy Problem was proposed in 2012 by Dr. Damian Milton.
It posited that Autistic people do not lack empathy; there is a gap between Autistic and non-Autistic experience that means neither group can understand the others experience well enough to truly empathise. This is then results in communication breakdown and interpersonal conflict.
The Double Empathy Problem could be applied to any experience of neurodivergence
We can not truly know an experience we do not have
Therefore, when a co-worker or employee is disclosing struggles or a need for accommodation, they should be considered the expert on their experience.

posts.title: Acquired Neurodivergence and workplace: Masking/Camoflauging
posts.text:
Masking/Camoflauging
Many neurodivergent people mask or camouflage their traits and struggles as a survival mechanism
It is not an active choice, and is often something we have spent a long time learning to do reflexively
This costs a lot of energy, and by creating supportive environments we can move to improve each others wellbeing by reducing the need to mask our struggles

Victimisation & Bullying
“Our findings showed that a lot of autistic people think it is normal to be hurt by people you know because it has happened to them so much. This makes many autistic people feel like they need to mask parts of themselves to stay safe, but this also makes them really exhausted. It took some people a long time to realise what had happened to them was wrong, and it was hard to ask for help. People who did ask for help often had bad experiences with professionals (e. g. police) who did not know much about autistic people.” (Pearson et al, 2022)
For many neurodivergent people (not just Autistic people), workplace bullying is a common concern. A workplace is not truly accessible if neurodivergent or otherwise disabled people experience bullying or discrimination from people in their work environment.
Pearson, A. , Rose, K. , & Rees, J. (2023). Autism, 27(2), 500-511.

posts.title: An Intro To The Ecosystemic Model Of Distress
posts.deck: An Intro To The Ecosystemic Model Of Distress
posts.text:
An Intro To The Ecosystemic Model Of Distress

How this session works
Content note: we will discuss burnout, trauma, psychosis, coercive care and exploitation. Leave, move, stim, or look away at any point.
Who this is for: Autistic and neurodivergent people, families, and professionals - in the same room, on purpose. The model is meant to be usable by all three.
What you'll leave with: one question you can apply anywhere - what is this distress responding to?

Where do we locate distress?
Because where we locate it determines what we try to fix.
Medical Model – Distress inside the person
Social Model – Distress arising from barriers to wellbeing
Ecosystemic model – Distress arising from complex variables across all environments including the bodymind

A century of looking inward
Dominant Western mental health has worked from one assumption: that distress lives inside the individual - faulty chemistry, disordered cognition, personal dysfunction.
Correction - change the thinking.
Compliance - change the behaviour.
Coping - build tolerance for harm.
Cure - remove the difference.
None of this is relevant or helpful to the contemporary understanding of neurodivergence

posts.title: An Intro To The Ecosystemic Model Of Distress: Politically convenient. Administratively tidy.
posts.deck: An Intro To The Ecosystemic Model Of Distress
posts.text:
Politically convenient. Administratively tidy.
If the problem is inside the person, then the person has to change. No school redesigns its day. No ward changes its lighting. No policy is rewritten. No budget moves.
This individualised model has been extraordinarily useful to systems.
It has also failed. Outcomes for Autistic and otherwise neurodivergent people have not improved in step with awareness, diagnosis, or service investment.

We are not sealed units
We are responsive, relational, ecological beings.
This is the starting premise of the ecosystemic model.
This requires is to look at distress as a product of intersecting environments.

Three nested, leaking levels
An ecosystem is not one environment. It is many environments, nested inside one another, operating at the same time.
They do not stay in their lanes. Pressure at one level reshapes experience at the others. Relief at one level can stabilise the whole system.
Level 3 - Systems
Level 2 - Immediate
Level 1 - Bodymind

Level 1: The inner environment - the bodymind
We exist in the environment of our bodymind at all times. Distress is always embodied.
Pain, nausea, hunger, breath, temperature
How those signals get interpreted and given meaning
Chronic illness, injury, disability, fatigue, sleep
Trauma and stress physiology; activation and shutdown
The key move: distress often appears first here, but appearing here is not originating here. The bodymind is simply where mismatch becomes unavoidable.
When the signals are overridden, disbelieved, or pathologised, distress intensifies as needs remain unmet.

posts.title: An Intro To The Ecosystemic Model Of Distress: Level 2: The immediate ecosystem - what we're placed inside
posts.deck: An Intro To The Ecosystemic Model Of Distress
posts.text:
Level 2: The immediate ecosystem - what we're placed inside
Sensory: sound, light, smell, touch, movement, visual load, unpredictability. What barely registers for one nervous system floods another.
Physical: access, layout, crowding, seating, toilets, exits, temperature. An inaccessible environment isn't neutral - it actively produces distress and is often dictated by power structures and policies.
Predictability and cognitive load: routine, transitions, clarity, pacing, task-switching, executive demand. Previewing and choice are load-bearing supports.
Relational: attunement or misattunement. Co-regulation or control. Dignity or shame. Being believed or dismissed. Rupture repaired or left to fester.
This is the level most often misread as "behaviour". Conflict between others in our environment affects us too - even when it isn't about us.

Level 3: The systems ecosystem - where power lives
Schools, workplaces, healthcare systems
Policy, rules, thresholds, eligibility criteria
Economic conditions and cultural normativity
Ableism, racism, sexism, classism
Diagnostic gatekeeping and histories of exclusion
What Level 3 decides: whose distress is taken seriously. Whose pain is minimised. Whose needs are framed as unreasonable. Whose survival is made conditional.
Level 3 never stays abstract. It flows downward - shaping the Level 2 environments people are placed inside, and how they are treated within them. It also shapes how we relate to our own bodymind at Level 1.

posts.title: An Intro To The Ecosystemic Model Of Distress: Distress as cumulative mismatch
posts.deck: An Intro To The Ecosystemic Model Of Distress
posts.text:
Distress as cumulative mismatch
Mismatch at Level 3: a policy, a threshold, a cut, an assumption about what counts as a real need.
increases pressure at Level 2: the room gets louder, the day gets less predictable, the relationship gets more controlling.
which overwhelms the bodymind at Level 1: pain, exhaustion, shutdown, dissociation, collapse.
We then try to fix it at Level 1. This is why interventions so often fail - and why people get blamed for not improving.

Systemic backflow
Even when distress appears to start low in the ecosystem, Level 3 shapes how it is experienced, responded to, and remembered.
Past harm alters future physiology. Dismissal today increases vulnerability tomorrow. Systems teach bodyminds what to expect.
Harm moves downward through the ecosystem - then cycles back upward as crisis, burnout, withdrawal, collapse.
What looks like personal failure is usually ecosystemic exhaustion.

Change the question
The medical model asks: "What is wrong with this person?"
The ecosystemic model asks: "What is this distress responding to?"
Burnout, substance use, dissociation, anxiety, even psychosis - these are not meaningless symptoms. They are feedback: signals that something in the ecosystem has become unsustainable.
This does not reject medicine. It contextualises it. It does not minimise suffering. It makes sense of it.

posts.title: An Intro To The Ecosystemic Model Of Distress: Then healing is ecosystem repair
posts.deck: An Intro To The Ecosystemic Model Of Distress
posts.text:
Then healing is ecosystem repair
Environmental: sensory access, predictability, continuity of attention, material security.
Relational: co-regulation, belonging, reduced neuronormative pressure, repair after rupture.
Institutional: neurodivergence-competent practice, ethical policy, reduced coercion.
Political: social safety nets, disability justice, poverty reduction.
Cultural: valuing lived experience, dismantling deficit narratives.
The shift: healing becomes a collective responsibility, not a private burden.

What this asks of us
If you are Autistic
Your distress is not evidence of defect. It is evidence of mismatch.
Recovery you are asked to do alone, in unchanged conditions, is not recovery.
Energy accounting is a map of what is costing you - not a discipline you're failing at.
Community is an environmental intervention.
If you work in a system
Ask what environment this person is being asked to survive, before you ask what's wrong with them.
Support the bodymind rather than overriding it.
Reshape environments rather than building endurance.
Notice when your service is the Level 3 pressure.
Accommodation is not indulgence. Access is not special treatment. Safety is not optional.

posts.title: Autism 101 NeuroHub: Autism 101
posts.text:
Autism 101
for Professionals
Understanding Autistic experience through a neurodiversity-affirming lens
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org

Forget everything you have ever read about autism.
— Dr Luke Beardon

What We Will Cover Today
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
Rethinking Autism: Models and Frameworks
The Autistic Ecosystem
How Autistic Minds Work
Masking and Its Consequences
Autistic Burnout
Language, Identity and Professional Practice

PART 1
Rethinking Autism
Models, paradigms, and why it matters which lens we use
(Speaker notes: Before we can talk about Autistic experience, we need to examine the lenses through which professionals are taught to see it. Not all frameworks are equal — and some cause direct harm.)

posts.title: Autism 101 NeuroHub: Two Models of Disability: Which One Shapes Your Practice?
posts.text:
Two Models of Disability: Which One Shapes Your Practice?
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
Medical Model – Pathology Paradigm
Locates the problem inside the person
Autism = deficit, disorder, impairment
Goal: normalise, remediate, fix
Autistic people are passive objects of intervention
Progress measured by how closely person approximates neurotypical norms
Drives harmful therapies (ABA, 'social skills' training)
Social & Ecosystemic Model - Neurodiversity Paradigm
Locates the problem in the ecosystem mismatch
Autism = a different neurotype with different needs
Goal: understand, accommodate, affirm
Autistic people are active experts in their own experience
Progress measured by wellbeing, autonomy and belonging
Drives inclusive practice, adjustments, advocacy
(Speaker notes: The model you operate from determines everything — what questions you ask, what outcomes you pursue, and whose knowledge you trust. The neurodiversity paradigm does not deny that Autistic people face challenges. It asks where those challenges come from, and who is responsible for addressing them.)

posts.title: Autism 101 NeuroHub: Theories We Have Left Behind (and Why)
posts.text:
Theories We Have Left Behind (and Why)
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
These theories remain in circulation. They should not shape your practice.
Theory of Mind deficit
Claim that Autistic people cannot mentalise. Disproven by the Double Empathy Problem — the difficulty is cross-neurotype, not one-sided.
Weak Central Coherence
Framed Autistic attention as deficit. Monotropism offers a far more accurate and non-pathologising account of Autistic attention.
Extreme Male Brain
Gendered, biologistic, and fails to account for the majority of Autistic people. Fuelled decades of missed diagnoses in women and non-binary people.
Executive Dysfunction model
Describes observed differences as 'deficits'. Does not account for the context-dependence and demand-sensitivity of Autistic executive function.
Refrigerator Mother / Bad Parenting
Autism is not caused by cold or emotionally unavailable parenting. This theory caused — and continues to cause — immense harm to families.
MMR Vaccine causation
Comprehensively debunked. Based on fraudulent research. Should never appear in professional discourse.
(Speaker notes: Each of these theories positions Autistic people as broken versions of neurotypical people. None of them are unique, universal, or specific to Autistic experience. Their persistence in practice causes real harm.)

posts.title: Autism 101 NeuroHub: The Pathology Paradigm vs The Neurodiversity Paradigm
posts.text:
The Pathology Paradigm vs The Neurodiversity Paradigm
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
Dimension
Pathology Paradigm
Neurodiversity Paradigm
Origin of difficulty
Within the person — deficit of brain function
In the ecosystem — mismatch between neurotype and environment
Role of the professional
Expert diagnosing and treating the patient
Collaborator supporting the person to navigate their ecosystem
Goal of intervention
Reduce Autistic traits; achieve neurotypical functioning
Reduce ecosystem barriers; increase safety, belonging, autonomy
Whose knowledge counts
Clinical observation and diagnostic criteria
Lived experience, community knowledge, and research done with Autistic people
(Speaker notes: The paradigm shift is not merely semantic. It changes who does the work, who is considered the expert, and what counts as success. Autistic advocates and researchers have been making this argument for decades. We are listening.)

PART 2
The Autistic Ecosystem
Understanding Autistic experience as shaped by nested environments
(Speaker notes: The ecosystemic model provides a framework for understanding why Autistic people experience the world the way they do — not as a feature of individual pathology, but as the product of a Bodymind existing in environments that were not designed for it.)

posts.title: Autism 101 NeuroHub: A Foundational Equation
posts.text:
A Foundational Equation
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
A Foundational Equation
Autism + Environment = Outcome
Luke Beardon (2020)
Autistic distress, difficulty, and apparent 'dysfunction' are not fixed properties of the Autistic person. They are the product of the interaction between the Autistic Bodymind and its environment. Change the environment, change the outcome.
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
(Speaker notes: This equation is the foundation of ecosystemic practice. It shifts professional responsibility. If outcome = Autism + environment, then professionals who shape environments have direct power over Autistic outcomes. That is not a minor point.)

posts.title: Autism 101 NeuroHub: The Ecosystemic Model: Three Nested Environments
posts.text:
The Ecosystemic Model: Three Nested Environments
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
POWER STRUCTURES
Healthcare systems  ·  Education  ·  Social services  ·  Law  ·  Diagnostic criteria  ·  Cultural norms
IMMEDIATE ENVIRONMENT
Family  ·  School / Workplace  ·  Home  ·  Community  ·  Professionals  ·  Peer relationships
BODYMIND
Neurology  ·  Sensory experience  ·  Emotion  ·  Identity  ·  Monotropic attention  ·  Interoception
The Autistic Bodymind in its ecosystem — not a broken person in a neutral world.
(Speaker notes: The ecosystemic model tells us that Autistic experience cannot be understood by looking at the Autistic person in isolation. The Bodymind exists inside an Immediate Environment — home, school, workplace, community — which itself exists inside structures of Power — healthcare systems, diagnostic criteria, cultural norms about what a person should be. Distress arises in the interactions between these layers. Support must address all three levels, not just the Bodymind.)

posts.title: Autism 101 NeuroHub: What Creates Autistic Distress: The Ecosystem at Work
posts.text:
What Creates Autistic Distress: The Ecosystem at Work
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
Autistic distress is not a symptom of Autism. It is the product of an ecosystem that does not fit.
Sensory environments
Designed for neurotypical sensory tolerance — fluorescent lighting, open-plan offices, noisy classrooms, unpredictable sounds.
Implicit social rules
Unspoken norms that neurotypical people absorb automatically but Autistic people must consciously identify, learn, and perform.
Demand to mask
Pressure to suppress Autistic responses and perform neurotypical behaviour — chronically depleting and traumatising.
Lack of predictability
Monotropic attention depends on knowing what is coming. Sudden changes, last-minute demands, and inconsistency are disproportionately costly.
Diagnostic and institutional gatekeeping
Criteria designed around male, white, non-masking presentations. Professionals who deny Autistic experience create a second layer of harm.
Epistemic injustice
The systematic dismissal of Autistic people as credible knowers of their own experience — from individual clinicians to entire healthcare systems.
(Speaker notes: Each of these stressors is produced by the ecosystem — not by Autism itself. Professionals can influence each of them through practice, advocacy, and how they design their environments and interactions.)

posts.title: Autism 101 NeuroHub: Autistic Trauma: A Product of the Ecosystem
posts.text:
Autistic Trauma: A Product of the Ecosystem
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
Trauma in Autistic people does not arise from Autism — it arises from what happens to Autistic people in hostile ecosystems.
Sensory Trauma
Repeated overwhelming sensory exposure without accommodation or exit.
Communication Trauma
Having communication styles consistently misread, pathologised, or ignored.
Gaslighting
Being told that experiences are not real, not that bad, or a product of one's own failing.
Monotropic Split
Being repeatedly pulled away from deep focus — a form of attentional distress specific to monotropic minds.
School Trauma
Educational environments that demand masking, social performance, and sensory tolerance without support.
Minority Stress
The chronic stress of existing as a marginalised neurotype in a world designed for another.
Institutional Betrayal
Being harmed by the very professionals and systems designed to help — clinicians who deny, dismiss, or misdiagnose.
Intergenerational Trauma
Unidentified Autistic parents and community members whose own unmet needs shape family environments.
(Speaker notes: The distinction between Autism and trauma caused by hostile responses to Autism is clinically and ethically important. When professionals confuse the two, they misattribute ecosystem harm to the person. Autistic people are not traumatised because they are Autistic. They are traumatised because the world is built for someone else.)

posts.title: Autism 101 NeuroHub: PART 3
posts.text:
PART 3
How Autistic Minds Work
Monotropism, the Double Empathy Problem, and sensory experience
(Speaker notes: This section moves from the ecosystem to the Bodymind — exploring the theories that actually explain Autistic cognition and experience, replacing deficit models with accurate accounts.)

Monotropism: The Only Theory That Accounts for All of Autism
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
Monotropism proposes that all people have finite attentional resources. Autistic people channel those resources into a narrow, deeply focused attention tunnel — rather than distributing them broadly.
POLYTROPIC (non-Autistic)
The Flashlight
Wide beam · many interests · shallow depth · easily split
↔
MONOTROPIC (Autistic)
The Laser
Narrow beam · deep focus · rich detail · costly to shift
What monotropism explains:
Focused interests — deep engagement with fewer topics
Autistic inertia — difficulty initiating, transitioning, and switching tasks
Monotropic split — the distress of being pulled away from deep focus
Why demands and interruptions are disproportionately costly
Why sensory input that competes with focus is overwhelming
Murray, Lesser & Lawson (2005)
(Speaker notes: Monotropism is the only theory of Autism that accounts for every aspect of Autistic experience. It was developed by Autistic researchers. It is not a deficit model — it describes a different attentional style with different costs and different strengths.)

posts.title: Autism 101 NeuroHub: The Double Empathy Problem
posts.text:
The Double Empathy Problem
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
The Double Empathy Problem does not say Autistic people lack empathy. It says that empathy is harder across neurotypes — in both directions.
“Autistic people do not have a deficit or inability to mentalise. There is a cross-neurotype mismatch at play. Those with a predominant neurotype (PNT) easily empathise with other PNT people due to shared experiences. This fails in cross-neurotype interaction — on both sides.”
Milton (2012)
What this means for practice:
Non-Autistic people are equally poor at understanding Autistic people — but are not pathologised for it
PNT professionals carry unconscious bias about Autistic communication — hearing it as rude, cold, or difficult
Autistic people who communicate directly are experiencing the double empathy gap, not a social deficit
This is a key driver of bullying, victimisation, and professional misread
(Speaker notes: This fundamentally changes the professional's role. If the empathy gap runs in both directions, the professional cannot treat their own reading of Autistic communication as objective. They must actively work to understand it.)

posts.title: Autism 101 NeuroHub: Sensory Processing: Beyond the Five Senses
posts.text:
Sensory Processing: Beyond the Five Senses
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
Autistic sensory processing is not simply about being 'sensitive'. It is about how the Bodymind integrates information from eight sensory channels.
Visual
Fluorescent flicker, visual clutter, bright light, movement in periphery
Auditory
Background noise, multiple voices, unexpected sounds, hyperacusis
Tactile
Clothing textures, tags, light touch, proprioceptive seeking
Olfactory
Perfumes, food, cleaning products — scent is impossible to avoid
Gustatory
Texture, temperature, flavour profile — ARFID frequently linked to sensory profile
Vestibular
Balance, movement, need for movement or stillness (stimming)
Proprioceptive
Body position in space — seeking or avoiding deep pressure, movement
Interoceptive
Internal signals: hunger, thirst, pain, temperature, heartbeat, emotion
(Speaker notes: Sensory differences are universal in Autistic experience. They can involve hyper-sensitivity, hypo-sensitivity, or both across different channels. Environments designed without sensory awareness create chronic distress before the Autistic person has even attempted any other task.)

posts.title: Autism 101 NeuroHub: Interoception and Alexithymia: The Internal Landscape
posts.text:
Interoception and Alexithymia: The Internal Landscape
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
Interoception — the sense of the body's internal state — is frequently atypical in Autistic people. This has profound consequences for daily life.
Hunger / Thirst
May not receive reliable internal signals — leading to missed meals, dehydration, and confusion about physical need.
Pain and Illness
May not recognise pain signals until they reach a high threshold — leading to apparent 'high pain tolerance' or delayed help-seeking.
Emotion identification
Alexithymia (difficulty identifying emotions) affects a significant proportion of Autistic people. Emotion may be experienced as physical sensation only.
Having a switch, not a dial
Interoceptive signals may arrive abruptly at full intensity rather than gradually — making regulation harder and crises more likely.
Hyper-empathy
Some Autistic people experience overwhelming empathic sensitivity — absorbing others' emotional states without regulation. Often misread as 'over-reaction'.
Interoceptive stimming
Some stimming behaviours are attempts to generate or attend to internal signals — to know the body's state.
(Speaker notes: Interoceptive differences are frequently missed in professional assessment. They have significant implications for healthcare, emotional support, and understanding behaviour. An Autistic person who 'doesn't seem to notice' they are distressed may literally not be receiving the internal signal clearly.)

posts.title: Autism 101 NeuroHub: Focused Interests: Depth, Not Deficit
posts.text:
Focused Interests: Depth, Not Deficit
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
What are often described as 'obsessions' or 'restricted interests' are more accurately understood through monotropism: deep, rich engagement that reflects the Autistic attentional profile.
Focused interests are a source of joy, identity, expertise, and regulation — not a pathological feature to be reduced
They connect Autistic people to community, purpose, and wellbeing
Restricting or suppressing focused interests removes a primary source of regulation and can accelerate burnout
They may change over time, expand, contract, or intensify depending on the person's wider ecosystem
Professionals who dismiss focused interests as 'not real' communication are missing the most direct window into the person
Practice implication:
Ask about focused interests early. Use them as communication bridges. Incorporate them into support planning. Understand them as a map to the person's identity, not a quirk to be managed.
(Speaker notes: The language professionals use here matters. 'Obsession' is pejorative and framed through a medical lens. 'Focused interest' is accurate and non-pathologising. This is not just semantics — it shapes how the professional relates to the Autistic person and whether they create trust or distress.)

posts.title: Autism 101 NeuroHub: PART 4
posts.text:
PART 4
Masking and Its Consequences
The hidden cost of performing neurotypicality
(Speaker notes: Masking is the single most important concept for professionals to understand if they work with Autistic people. It explains why you may not 'see' Autism in a professional setting — and why what you don't see may be causing profound harm.)

Masking: Definition and Scope
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
“Autistic masking — also referred to in the literature as camouflaging, compensation, and most recently ‘adaptive morphing’ — is the conscious or unconscious suppression of natural responses and adoption of alternatives across a range of domains including social interaction, sensory experience, cognition, movement, and behaviour.”
Pearson & Rose (2021)
Masking is not deception. It is survival.
It may be conscious, unconscious, or both simultaneously
It is learned in response to social environments that punish Autistic behaviour
It applies across ALL domains — not just social interaction
It is more common in people who received late diagnoses, women, non-binary people, and those from marginalised communities
Professionals who see a 'well-functioning' person may be seeing an expert masker in crisis
(Speaker notes: The implications for assessment are enormous. A person who masks effectively in a 40-minute clinical appointment may receive a completely different picture to the one their daily life presents. Assessment must go beyond what is observable in the room.)

posts.title: Autism 101 NeuroHub: The Cost of Masking: Why This Matters Clinically
posts.text:
The Cost of Masking: Why This Matters Clinically
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
Chronic exhaustion
Maintaining a neurotypical performance is metabolically expensive. Masking round the clock depletes cognitive and emotional resources.
Identity erosion
Long-term masking can result in profound confusion about who one actually is — particularly when masking begins in early childhood.
Missed or delayed diagnosis
If the Autistic person presents as 'coping' in assessment, diagnostic criteria may not appear to be met. Women and girls are particularly affected.
Acceleration of burnout
Masking is a primary driver of Autistic burnout. As the energy budget is depleted, masking becomes impossible — this is often misread as sudden 'deterioration'.
Relationship to mental health
High levels of masking are significantly associated with depression, anxiety, suicidality, and lower quality of life.
Inauthentic support
If support is designed for the masked presentation, it is designed for someone who does not exist. It will fail — and the Autistic person will be blamed for its failure.
(Speaker notes: Masking is not a neutral adaptation. It is a chronic stressor with profound clinical consequences. Professionals who celebrate Autistic people for 'coping well' or 'not seeming Autistic' are inadvertently rewarding masking — which accelerates the harm.)

posts.title: Autism 101 NeuroHub: PART 5
posts.text:
PART 5
Autistic Burnout
Understanding the ecosystem collapse — not a mood disorder
(Speaker notes: Autistic burnout is one of the most frequently missed and misunderstood presentations in clinical settings. It is not depression. It is not regression. It is the consequence of an Autistic person's ecosystem consistently exceeding their capacity.)

Autistic Burnout: Definition
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
“When an Autistic person regularly exceeds their energy budget, this can lead to burnout, which may result in a lessened ability to function daily and an increased observability of Autistic traits.”
Raymaker et al. (2020)
Observable features (Arnold et al. , 2023; Higgins et al. , 2021):
Cognitive overload and monotropic split — severe difficulty switching or initiating
Severe mental and physical exhaustion disproportionate to apparent cause
Interpersonal withdrawal — reduced capacity for all social interaction
Significant reduction in functioning across multiple areas simultaneously
Increased intensity of Autistic traits and/or complete loss of capacity to mask
Confusion, dissociation, executive dysfunction
(Speaker notes: Burnout is qualitatively different from depression, though the two can co-occur. The key difference is that burnout is specifically triggered by ecosystem overload, and recovery requires ecosystem change — not medication or talking therapy alone.)

posts.title: Autism 101 NeuroHub: Atypical Burnout: When People Can't Stop
posts.text:
Atypical Burnout: When People Can't Stop
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
Not all burnout looks like shutdown. Autistic burnout can present as hyperactivation — commonly called 'Meerkat Mode'.
“The use of the word atypical is not to create a neat category for an observable form of burnout. What we are referring to is burnout that might look different to the typical 'depressive' understanding. In our experience it is not at all rare or atypical. We come across this time and again.”
Atypical burnout may look like:
Hyperactivity, racing thoughts, inability to rest or stop
Frantic task-switching rather than shutdown or stillness
Apparent 'energy' that masks complete internal depletion
Frequently co-occurring with ADHD presentations — AuDHD profile
Misread as 'fine', 'not burned out', or 'attention-seeking'
(Speaker notes: Meerkat mode is particularly important for professionals to understand because it is the burnout presentation most likely to be missed or misread. The person looks busy and functional. They are not. They are running on empty at high speed.)

posts.title: Autism 101 NeuroHub: Why Observational Models of Burnout Fall Short
posts.text:
Why Observational Models of Burnout Fall Short
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
The progress we have made in understanding Autistic experience has come from Autistic people — not from observational, deficit-based approaches.
Observational models miss the interior
Burnout is fundamentally an internal, experienced state. What can be observed from the outside is not the same thing.
'Female autism' framing
Concepts like 'female autism' pathologise gender difference. Masking patterns are not female — they are a response to particular social environments.
Medical model focus
Observational models continue to locate the problem within the person. They do not account for ecosystem drivers.
Conflation with depression
Burnout and depression require different responses. Treating burnout as depression misses its cause and may prolong it.
“There are infinite possible interactions between a monotropic person and their environment. And this is why we often struggle to define our experiences through something that can be outwardly observed and measured.” — Adkin (2023)
(Speaker notes: The Autistic community has been ahead of clinical research on burnout for years. Double empathy, masking, stimming, interoception, exposure anxiety — all understood first through lived experience, then validated by research. This is a reason to take community knowledge seriously as a professional.)

posts.title: Autism 101 NeuroHub: Demand Avoidance: PDA Profile
posts.text:
Demand Avoidance: PDA Profile
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
Pathological Demand Avoidance — more accurately framed as Persistent Drive for Autonomy — describes a profile in which demand avoidance is pervasive, driven by anxiety and threat response, and qualitatively different from 'ordinary' Autistic demand sensitivity.
Demand Trauma Response
Demands trigger a threat response. The nervous system interprets demands as danger, not inconvenience.
Hyper-arousal baseline
The autonomic nervous system is running at higher baseline activation — making regulation harder and thresholds lower.
People-focused
PDA profiles are often highly attuned to people — watching for threat signals, reading social dynamics with precision.
Role play and fantasy
Identity fluidity and engagement with fictional or fantastical frameworks for self — may reduce the threat of demands by stepping outside 'self'.
Masking and social drive
Many PDA profiles have high social drive alongside social difficulty — they want connection but are easily overwhelmed by it.
Lack of stable sense of self
Identity may feel fragmented or highly context-dependent — making consistent demand response hard to establish.
(Speaker notes: PDA is frequently misread as ODD (Oppositional Defiant Disorder), conduct disorder, or attachment disorder. Conventional behaviour management strategies often worsen the profile significantly. Low-demand, high-autonomy approaches are most effective.)

posts.text:
PART 6
Language, Identity and Professional Practice
What we say shapes what we see — and what we do
(Speaker notes: Language is not peripheral to professional practice. The words professionals use determine the framework they operate in, the questions they ask, and the power dynamics they create or challenge.)

posts.title: Autism 101 NeuroHub: Identity-First Language: Why It Matters
posts.text:
Identity-First Language: Why It Matters
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
The Autistic community has a clear, consistent, and well-evidenced preference: identity-first language.
Identity-First (IFL)
“An Autistic person”
Autism is part of identity — not separate from the person
Consistent with Deaf community and disability rights practice
Preferred by the majority of Autistic people
Person-First (PFL)
“A person with autism”
Implies Autism is separate from and lesser than the person
Developed without significant Autistic community input
Found offensive by many Autistic people
This is not just preference — it is an expression of epistemic justice. Use the language the person in front of you uses for themselves. Default to IFL in the absence of stated preference.
Autism is not caused by vaccines, bad parenting, heavy metals, parasites, or brain damage — never imply otherwise
Autism is not a superpower — this is a reductive, unhelpful framing that erases real difficulty
Autism is not a spectrum from 'low' to 'high functioning' — functioning labels are contextual, misleading, and dehumanising
(Speaker notes: Every professional in this room will work with Autistic people who have been harmed by language — who have been called high-functioning and subsequently denied support, or called low-functioning and denied autonomy. Language is not neutral.)

posts.title: Autism 101 NeuroHub: Language to Retire From Professional Practice
posts.text:
Language to Retire From Professional Practice
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
These phrases are in common use. They cause harm. They should not appear in professional communication about Autistic people.
Everyone's a little bit Autistic
Trivialises Autistic experience and implies a continuum with neurotypicality that does not exist.
Challenging behaviour
Centred the perspective of the observer. Describes the Autistic person as the problem. Does not ask what the behaviour communicates.
Mum's anxiety / Mum reports
Dismisses parental observation and pathologises the reporter. Part of institutionalised parent blame.
High/Low functioning
Functioning varies by context, demand, and day. Labels deny support to those deemed 'high' and autonomy to those deemed 'low'.
Fine in school
Masking is higher in formal settings. School 'okayness' with home meltdown is a classic pattern of deferred burnout, not evidence of capability.
Autism is a superpower
Romanticises while erasing real suffering. Autistic people are allowed to find Autism genuinely hard.
Resilience
Places the burden of adaptation on the Autistic person. The ecosystem should accommodate — the person should not be required to absorb its failure.
Deficit / Impairment / Disorder
Locates the problem in the person. Replace with 'difference', 'need', or direct description of what the person experiences.
(Speaker notes: For each of these: this is not about policing language. It is about understanding that language embeds assumptions — and those assumptions shape clinical decisions, referral choices, and whether an Autistic person is believed, supported, or turned away.)

posts.title: Autism 101 NeuroHub: Institutionalised Parent Blame and the FII Risk
posts.text:
Institutionalised Parent Blame and the FII Risk
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
One of the most harmful patterns in professional practice involving Autistic children and families is the attribution of the child's difficulties to parenting — rather than to unmet Autistic need.
Parents — particularly mothers — are frequently blamed for behaviours that are Autistic responses to an unaccommodating environment
Advocacy for appropriate support is sometimes reframed as 'inducement of illness' (FII / MSBP concerns)
This pattern is more common in families from marginalised communities and where the parent is also Autistic or neurodivergent
Phrases like 'Mum's anxiety' and 'Mum reports' embed parent-blame into clinical documentation
The parent's observations are often the most accurate source of information about the child's actual functioning — they should be treated as data, not pathology
Before raising FII concerns: ask whether the child has been appropriately assessed for Autistic and other neurodivergent needs. Ask whether the environment has been accommodated. Ask whether the parent's account has been genuinely heard. In many cases, parental distress is a rational response to a child in an unaccommodating system.
(Speaker notes: This is not an abstract concern. Families are being harmed by institutional responses that pathologise appropriate advocacy. Professionals need to examine their own assumptions about what 'a concerned parent' looks like — and whose concerns they treat as credible.)

posts.title: Autism 101 NeuroHub: Rethinking the Spectrum: Not a Line, Not a Hierarchy
posts.text:
Rethinking the Spectrum: Not a Line, Not a Hierarchy
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
The Autism spectrum was never designed to be a linear scale from 'mild' to 'severe'. That understanding is both inaccurate and harmful.
The linear model (wrong)
Mild → Moderate → Severe
Implies a single dimension of 'how Autistic'
Used to deny or limit support
Erases individual profiles completely
The profile model (accurate)
Multidimensional · Contextual
Each Autistic person has a unique sensory, social, and attentional profile
Functioning varies by context and day
Consolidation of DSM-5 (2013) removed prior subtype labels
A person may be highly verbal and academically accomplished while in crisis at home. A person may have minimal spoken language and profound support needs while having rich inner experience. The spectrum cannot be read from the outside.
Retire: Kanner's Autism, Asperger's (clinical), HFA/LFA, PDD-NOS. These labels are no longer in use — and their lingering use signals outdated practice.
(Speaker notes: The consolidation of Autism subtypes in the DSM-5 was not perfect, but it did remove the diagnostic fiction of a spectrum from less to more Autistic. What we have instead is a population of people with enormously varied profiles, all of whom are unambiguously Autistic.)

Autistic people are not broken. We are people whose Bodymind exists in an ecosystem that was not designed for us. Your job is not to fix us — it is to understand us, and to change the ecosystem.
— NeuroHub Community Ltd.

The Theory of Monotropism
The theory of monotropism tells us that each person, regardless of neurotype has finite attentional resources.
It suggests that Autistic people’s attention is more laser focussed whereas non-autistic people are described as polytropic, meaning they can spread their attention across multiple interests but in much shallower detail.

posts.title: Autism and psychosis: Autism and Psychosis
posts.text:
Autism and Psychosis

How common is psychosis for autistic people?
While psychosis is not a defining characteristic of autism, research suggests we are more prone to psychosis. As many as 24% of Autistic people may experience psychosis (Kiyono et al, 2020)
This stands in comparison to research in the general population that suggests a lifetime prevalence of 7. 8% (Staines et al, 2022)

Why is psychosis so common in Autistic people?
60% of Autistic people report experiencing PTSD at some poin in their life (Rumball et al, 2020)
It has been suggested that PTSD occurs in as many as 40% of people with first-episode psychosis (Mueser et al, 2008)
(Speaker notes: Monotropism is the most universal theory that explains Autistic experience. Previous theories have only existed to name observable things.)

The burnout to psychosis cycle

Psychosis

What is it like to be Autistic and Psychotic?
Many of us will have masked for many years.
Because of this, we are likely to do better at masking our psychosis.
It took a further 2 years to start medication.
(Speaker notes: (Reference burnout literature) Quote literature)

Why did it take so long to get diagnosed?
Doctors did not understand Autistic experiences
Doctors didn’t believe autism and schizophrenia could occur together

posts.text:
How can you support Autistic people experiencing psychosis?
Believe us.
Do not make assumptions or comments based on our level of insight, we have been pretending to be okay our whole lives.
Get a diagnosis in place as quickly as is reasonably possible.
Avoid group therapy.
Be aware that we may be more prone to medication side effects.

Autistic Burnout, Psychosis, and the Ecology of Distress
From Disconnection to Breakdown: Rethinking Mental Health as Acquired Neurodivergence

Experienced consultant and mentor of 10 years
Award winning neurodiversity professional specialising in complex mentalhealth needs in the Autistic population
Registered mindfulness teacher
Published academic (recent papers on autism and substance use)
Multiply published author
Academic interests in mental health, critical theory, systems theory, and neuroqueer post-humanist studies

Why This Conversation Matters
Autistic burnout and psychosis are often treated as separate problems
What if they are part of the same ecosystemic process?
What if distress is not a failure of the individual, but a rupture in the human ecosystem?
How can addressing Autistic burnout support individuals into recovery from the distress of psychosis?

What The Research Says
While psychosis is not a defining characteristic of autism, research suggests we are more prone to psychosis. As many as 24% of Autistic people may experience psychosis (Kiyono et al, 2020)
This stands in comparison to research in the general population that suggests a lifetime prevalence of 7. 8% (Staines et al, 2022)

posts.title: Autistic Burnout, Psychosis, and the Ecology of Distress: Psychosis As Acquired Neurodivergence

posts.text:
Psychosis As Acquired Neurodivergence
Neurodivergence = a socio-political identity defined by one's distance from neuronormative performance (neurotypicality)
Includes both:
Innate neurodivergence — e. g. autism, ADHD
Acquired neurodivergence — e. g. trauma responses, psychosis, addiction
Acquired neurodivergence involves changes in cognition, perception, emotion, or identity that emerge over time
Often linked to: trauma, chronic stress, sensory overload, social disconnection

The Trauma Connection
60% of Autistic people report experiencing PTSD at some poin in their life (Rumball et al, 2020)
It has been suggested that PTSD occurs in as many as 40% of people with first-episode psychosis (Mueser et al, 2008)

The Ecosystemic Model Of Distress
Distress emerges across three indiscrete, interconnected layers
Bodymind Environment
Sleep, pain, interoception, trauma physiology
Immediate Environment
Sensory input, relationships, safety, predictability
Systems & Structures
Institutions, policy, stigma, access to resources

Distress As Ecological Breakdown
Distress is not internal failure
It is:
Accumulated survival pressures (minority stress)
Chronic invalidation
Loss of regulation across domains of the ecosystem

Understanding Autistic Burnout
Standard understanding as:
Chronic exhaustion
Loss of skills
Reduced tolerance to stimuli
Increased shutdown/meltdown
Better understood as a state of intense disconnection from bodymind, community, and support mechanisms:
Autistic burnout is not easily accurately described in symptomatic terms

To Psychosis

The Cycle

A self-reinforcing loop

Breaking The Cycle
We don’t “fix the person” We restore the ecosystem:
Bodymind:
Rest, nourishment, regulation
Environment:

Support, dignity, autonomy

Reframing Recovery
Recovery is not:
Returning to “normal”

Reconnection

Building sustainable ways of being

Conclusion Summary
Burnout and psychosis are not isolated conditions

Understanding this changes everything about how we respond

posts.deck: Autistic people and drug and alcohol use
posts.text:
Autistic People and Drug and Alcohol Use

Why do Autistic people use
drugs?
To understand this we must first understand Autistic experience.
In this section we will briefly cover-
Monotropism
Interoceptive Stimming
Energy Accounting and Burnout
Masking
The Double Empathy Problem
Autistic Sensory Trauma
Victimisation of Autistic individuals

Monotropism
Monotropism is considered the most universal and unifying autism theory.
Autistic people’s brains tend towards singular, hyperfocused attention tunnels, and have limited attentional resources to allocate to tasks (Murray et al, 2005) .
As opposed to neurotypical people who are able to split their attentional resources across multiple competing demands simultaneously.
Monotropism explains Autistic inertia.
(Speaker notes: Monotropism is the most universal theory that explains Autistic experience. Previous theories have only existed to name observable things.)

Interoceptive Stimming
Autistic people engage in “stimming”, or repetitive behaviours that help them stay regulated
For Autistic people with interoceptive differences, it can be difficult to identify and articulate emotional experiences
Drugs and alcohol allow the Autistic person to induce or block out certain feelings and emotions
Autistic people can use this as a stim, repeatedly triggering the same interoceptive feeling

posts.title: Autistic people and drug and alcohol use: Masking
posts.deck: Autistic people and drug and alcohol use
posts.text:
Masking
This is also known as ‘camouflaging’.
It refers to the act of concealing one’s Autistic traits to appear more neurotypical.
It is not necessarily a conscious choice, it is a survival reflex.
Masking takes a tremendous toll on cognitive and attentional resources and energy.
Many Autistic people are missed because they have become so adept at masking (Pearson & Rose, 2021).
(Speaker notes: (Reference burnout literature) Quote literature)

Energy Accounting and Burnout
Energy accounting is the concept that Autistic people have to manage their psychological and physical energy levels (or cognitive resources) throughout the day.
AKA ‘Spoon Theory’.
When an Autistic person regularly exceeds their energy budget, this can lead to Burnout, which may result in a lessened ability to function daily and an increased observability of Autistic traits (Raymaker et al, 2020).
(Speaker notes: Cross-neurological communication mismatch)

The Double Empathy Problem
Autistic emotional and communicative reciprocity is not in deficit, but instead different to that of non-Autistic people.
This means that Autistic-Autistic communication works better than Autistic-Neurotypical communication.
Autistic people are labelled as disordered in this area because of neuronormativity and marginalisation (Milton, 2012).
Autistic communicators are perceived negatively by non-Autistic individuals (Sasson et al. , 2017; Anders et al. , 2016).

posts.title: Autistic people and drug and alcohol use: Autistic Sensory Trauma

Autistic people have individual sensory profiles.
What may be exciting and restorative for one, may trigger trauma responses in another.

Individuals

We experience mate crime, criminal exploitation, harassment, and structural oppression far more commonly than neurotypical people.
Autistic people also occupy other intersections of race, gender and sexual identity, disability, and class inequality. Any of these will compound the experience (Pearson et al, 2022).

posts.text:
How does this relate to Autistic
Drug use?
Autistic people can easily become singularly focused on drug use, especially if self-medicating a co-occurring mental health problem.
Drugs can reduce the effect of sensory trauma, and act as a “spoon extender” when burned out.
Autistic people may turn to drug use as a result of abuse or exploitation.
They may use drugs to feel better connected to a social group.
(Speaker notes: People under influence of drugs have less inhibitions, Autistic communication seems more natural Can become specific focused interest Link to support needs arising from other slides ADHD- Stimulants may have relieving effect)

How does this relate to Autistic
Drug use?
Can create a feeling of community-connectedness via a shared interest.
Reduces inhibitions in group dynamics making Autistic communication feel more natural.
Drugs do work (short-term), in meeting the needs of an Autistic person.

What is unique about Autistic
drug use?
Autistic drug users tend to gather a lot of information on the drugs that they take.
There are entire ‘psychonaut’ communities that discuss drug using experiences, this sort of online engagement tends to attract Autistic and otherwise Neurodivergent people.
We may treat ourselves like a living science experiment.
We may have markedly easier or harder times trying to cessate our drug use.
Often very unphased by consequences of drug use.

posts.text:
Minority Stress and Drug Use
Botha (2020) found that community-connectedness reduced the effects of minority stress in Autistic people.
Connecting Autistic people with their community improves wellbeing.
When we improve wellbeing, the harms of drug use can be mitigated.
Despite this, services often fail to signpost people to the Autistic community.
(Speaker notes: Burnout? Often conceptualised as depression and anxiety Research tends to have an “outside-in” perspective with little reference to newer theory)

What does the research say?
There is very little research on the topic of Autistic people and drug use.
The research that is out there is not generally done by Autistic researchers.
The most useful study in existence was by Weir et al (2021) and found that while Autistic people were less likely to report using drugs, we were more likely to report using drugs for self-medication of mental health issues.
Leaves the question of how many drug users are unidentified Autistic people.
More research is needed in this area, and that research needs to be informed by the wealth of Autistic experiences that are accessible online.

posts.title: Depathologising Mental Wellbeing
posts.text:
Depathologising Mental Wellbeing

Learning Objectives
Consider how mental wellbeing has been medicalised
Discuss what purpose the medicalisation of mental wellbeing serves
Think about the role of trauma in mental wellbeing
Understand mental wellbeing through the lens of neurodiversity

How has mental wellbeing been
medicalised?
Over the past century, human distress has been viewed through the lens of “mental illness”
A number of treatments have been developed to effectively normalise the mind of a person in distress
Despite this, outcomes in psychiatry have not improved in half a century

The Pathologisation of distress
The experience of distress has been centred as a problem within a person
In actual fact, it is the logical conclusion of traumatic experiences in a person’s life

Why has mental wellbeing been
medicalised?
Normative attitudes in society have resulted in the dehumanisation of bodyminds that exist outside of cultural standards of “normal”
Those deemed to have “abnormal psychology” are often the people who are unable to generate profit and pay taxes
Treatment of “mental illness” is a billion dollar industry
Neuronormativity has resulted in the belief that we must all adhere to one style of thought, feeling, and expression

What factors play a role in our
Mental wellbeing?
Our social environment
Our physical environment
Trauma we have experienced

posts.title: Depathologising Mental Wellbeing: What constitutes trauma
posts.text:
What constitutes trauma
We must reframe the traditional view of trauma
Trauma is anything that has made our environment feel unsafe
It is an event, or series of events, that frame our sense of Self through the need for survival
Trauma is relative
Different people find different things traumatic

How does this relate to mentalwellbeing?
Trauma and a need to survive in an unsuitable environment is often one of the most significant factors in the development of negative wellbeing
Trauma teaches our brain that we are not safe, and thus must act in the name of survival
This can be fight, flight, freeze, or fawn

How does this relate to mental
wellbeing?
When our brain is consistently trying to survive in an unsuitable environment, it alters the way we think about the environment and ourselves
This can manifest as anything from depression to psychosis

Mental wellbeing and neurodiversity
Since trauma alters the function of our brain, it is necessary to view so-called “mental illness” not as illness, but as acquired neurodivergence
Trauma causes our brain to diverge from cultural standards of normality
This opens up a conversation about making meaningful changes that can reduce distress

Acquired neurodivergence and mental wellbeing
When we begin to view “mental illness” as a form of acquired neurodivergence, we make a move away from medical models
We externalise the issue by viewing acquired neurodivergence as a result of environmental factors
This is vital for Autistic people who are already pathologised for their innate neurodivergence

posts.title: Depathologising Mental Wellbeing: The Golden Equation
posts.text:
The Golden Equation
(Dr. Luke Beardon)
Autism + Environment = Outcome
Doesn’t just apply to Autistic people
When we adjust a person’s environment to better suit their needs and boundaries, it reduces their distress

Summary
Medicalising mental “health” does not improve outcomes
Viewing this through the lens of neurodiversity allows us to externalise the problem into the environment, and reduce a person’s distress

History Is Something We’re Inside-(but we can challenge it)

posts.text:
Addiction, Autism, and PDA

Why do Autistic people use
drugs?
To understand this we must first understand Autistic experience.
In this section we will briefly cover-
Monotropism
Energy Accounting and Burnout
Masking
The Double Empathy Problem
Autistic Sensory Trauma
Victimisation of Autistic individuals
Deficit/Medical Model
Poor Self-Image/Identity

Monotropism
Monotropism is considered the most universal and unifying autism theory.
Autistic people’s brains tend towards singular, hyperfocused attention tunnels, and have limited attentional resources to allocate to tasks (Murray et al, 2005) .
As opposed to neurotypical people who are able to split their attentional resources across multiple competing demands simultaneously.
Monotropism explains Autistic inertia.
(Speaker notes: Monotropism is the most universal theory that explains Autistic experience. Previous theories have only existed to name observable things.)

Masking
This is also known as ‘camouflaging’.
It refers to the act of concealing one’s Autistic traits to appear more neurotypical.
It is not necessarily a conscious choice, it is a survival reflex.
Masking takes a tremendous toll on cognitive and attentional resources and energy.
Many Autistic people are missed because they have become so adept at masking (Pearson & Rose, 2021).

posts.title: Fundamentals of Autistic people and drug use: Energy Accounting and Burnout
posts.deck: Fundamentals of Autistic people and drug use
posts.text:
Energy Accounting and Burnout
Energy accounting is the concept that Autistic people have to manage their psychological and physical energy levels (or cognitive resources) throughout the day.
AKA ‘Spoon Theory’.
When an Autistic person regularly exceeds their energy budget, this can lead to Burnout, which may result in a lessened ability to function daily and an increased observability of Autistic traits (Raymaker et al, 2020).
(Speaker notes: (Reference burnout literature) Quote literature)

The Double Empathy Problem
Autistic emotional and communicative reciprocity is not in deficit, but instead different to that of non-Autistic people.
This means that Autistic-Autistic communication works better than Autistic-Neurotypical communication.
Autistic people are labelled as disordered in this area because of neuronormativity and marginalisation (Milton, 2012).
Autistic communicators are perceived negatively by non-Autistic individuals (Sasson et al. , 2017; Anders et al. , 2016).
(Speaker notes: Cross-neurological communication mismatch)

Autistic Sensory Trauma
Autistic people have individual sensory profiles.
What may be exciting and restorative for one, may trigger trauma responses in another.
Sensory Trauma occurs when a sensory experience is overwhelming or painful for the Autistic person (Fulton et al, 2020).

posts.deck: Fundamentals of Autistic people and drug use
posts.text:
Victimisation of Autistic
Individuals
Autistic people are victimised at a higher rate than the general population.
We experience mate crime, criminal exploitation, harassment, and structural oppression far more commonly than neurotypical people.
Autistic people also occupy other intersections of race, gender and sexual identity, disability, and class inequality. Any of these will compound the experience (Pearson et al, 2022).

The Pathology Paradigm
The way that society views and speaks about Autistic people, as deficient and broken, has a direct negative impact on self-image and sense of identity.
The UK Autistic community prefers the neurodiversity paradigm, as this depathologises our existence.
There is a significant push to recognise disability as a form of oppression, rather than an issue centred in the individual (Walker, 2021).

Minority Stress and Drug Use
Minority stress is the name given to the effect of the cumulative stresses that members of a stigmatised and marginalised group experience.
It refers to the clustering of discriminatory experiences arising from structural marginalisation in society.
When we consider being Autistic as a minority identity, rather than the “disorder” of the pathology models, we can then start applying theories like minority stress to Autistic experience (Botha & Frost, 2020).

Minority Stress and Drug Use
Trauma is a leading factor in the development of drug use and dependency in individuals (Moustafa et al, 2021).
In order to reduce the harm of drug use in our community, we have to start by reducing minority stress.

posts.text:
Why is there a lack of research?
There is a misconception that Autistic people don’t take drugs.
We are infantilised by society for being disabled.
People assume that Autistic people love rules too much to take drugs.
There is also a belief that we lack access to spaces where drugs are available.
The largest issue is that Neurodivergent people are often misdiagnosed or unable to access diagnosis until after their drug use has stopped.
When we report these things, we are either too Autistic, or not Autistic enough to contribute to the conversation.
(Speaker notes: Schrodingers Autistic; either too Autistic to be reliable sources or not Autistic enough (Hudson) (Reference demirhetoricity Yergeau))

Minority Stress and Drug Use
Botha (2020) found that community-connectedness reduced the effects of minority stress in Autistic people.
Connecting Autistic people with their community improves wellbeing.
When we improve wellbeing, the harms of drug use can be mitigated.
Despite this, services often fail to signpost people to the Autistic community.

Addiction and PDA risk factors
People focused.
Often driven by the desire to fit in.
If no community is available, one will be found.
In the same way that double empathy means Autistic-Autistic communication works on shared culture, the same can be said of those in the addiction community.
30-50% of people dual diagnosed with substance dependence are neurodivergent (Gordon et al, 2004).

posts.title: Autistic people in inpatient care: Diagnosis
posts.text:
Diagnosis
EUPD was removed and Autism added approximately 6 months after second discharge
Schizophrenia was added as a diagnosis last year
ADHD was diagnosed last year
Correct medication for schizophrenia and ADHD has been life changing
Now approaching 9 years of sobriety
Relatively stable mental health
Able to work thanks to addition of ADHD medication

Staff Attitudes
Dismissive
Invalidating

Autistic Mental Health (Community Discourse)

Key Concepts
Monotropism
Masking
Energy Accounting and Autistic Burnout
The Double Empathy Problem
The Golden Equation

What is Monotropism?
The theory that Autistic people’s brains tend towards hyperfocused attention tunnels, and have limited attentional resources to allocate to tasks (Murray et al, 2005).
Rather than spread surface level attention across multiple stimuli and demands, Autistic people tend to put most or all of their attentional resources into one specific task.
This can look like anything from having a dedicated interest in computers, to perseverative thinking about a distressing idea.

posts.title: Autistic people in inpatient care: Monotropism & Mental Health
posts.text:
Monotropism & Mental Health
Monotropic Split: When an Autistic person is forced to apply their cognitive resources in a non-Autistic way, they experience monotropic split
This is like a cognitive trauma; we are being forced to live beyond our cognitive capacity
Autistic community positions this as a precursor to Autistic burnout and mental health issues
Monotropic Split is almost completely unavoidable for Autistic people
Society is not designed to accommodate Autistic attentional styles
Many Autistic people are also ADHD which further complicates the issue

Masking
Also known as ‘camouflaging’
Act of concealing one's Autistic traits in order to stay safe in an environment
Not necessarily a conscious choice, often reflexive
Many Autistic adults miss out on diagnosis due to masking (Pearson & Rose, 2023)
Represents an additional demand that can lead to monotropic split
Masking has been linked to
Autistic burnout
Mental health issues
Suicidality
Poor self-esteem
Difficulty with personal identity

posts.title: Autistic people in inpatient care: Energy Accounting & Burnout
posts.text:
Energy Accounting & Burnout
Energy accounting is the concept that Autistic people have to budget their psychological and physical energy levels (or cognitive resources) throughout the day.
Completing tasks and demands consumes that budget, and our wellbeing and self-care factor into what our budget is
When an Autistic person is forced to complete tasks that over-extend that energy budget, it can lead to burnout.
Extended periods of this can result in a debilitating state of fatigue, loss of skills, reduced ability to mask, and sensory & emotional dysregulation
Energy accounting is often referred to as ‘spoon theory’

Energy Accounting & Burnout
Autistic burnout can result in a wide range of outcomes
Particularly mental health issues and suicidality
Burnout is more than simply being tired
It is a total loss of skills and abilities that were previously usable

Monotropic Split
Forced to perform beyond cognitive resources
Burnout
Autistic person becomes burnt out
Hyper Vigilant State
Unable to feel safe; community calls this ‘meerkat mode’
Spiralling
Spiral monotropically on a subject that is distressing
Psychotic Phenomena
Autistic person experiences psychosis or psychotic-adjacent features
Burnout to Psychosis Cycle

The Golden Equation
Dr. Luke Beardon
Autism + Environment = Outcome
If we take Autistic people and put them into an environment that is not well suited to their needs, we can’t be surprised when they have a negative outcome.
If we want to see a positive outcome, we need to improve the environment, not the person.

posts.title: Autistic people in inpatient care: How This Changes Mental Health
posts.text:
How This Changes Mental Health
If a mental health problem is an outcome for a person, then it is not that they are ill or disordered
A mental health issue is the logical consequence of living in an environment that is not well suited to our needs
The more traumatic the environment, the worse the outcome
Through this, we can see mental health issues as ‘acquired neurodivergence’ rather than illness
The problem isn’t what is wrong with us, it’s what happened to us

The Double Empathy Problem
Posits that Autistic empathy, emotional, and communicative reciprocity is not in deficit, but instead different to that of non-Autistic people.
This means that Autistic-Autistic communication works better than Autistic-Neurotypical communication.
Autistic people are labelled as disordered in this area because of neuronormativity and marginalisation (Milton et al, 2023).
Autistic people in healthcare environments are often accuse of being rude or lacking emotions
This is caused by non-Autistic professionals failing to account for their different cultural experience of the world and not accounting for Autistic patients not having professional knowledge
Just because something is normal to you, does not mean it is known by the person.

How Does This Relate To Drug Use?
Self-Medicating
We may use drugs to cope with environments that are distressing
Stimming
We may use drugs because we enjoy the sensory experience
Community Seeking
We may use drugs to feel a level of community connectedness

posts.title: Autistic people in inpatient care: Self-Medicating
posts.text:
Self-Medicating
Autistic people in harmful environments will find ways of coping and masking their struggle in that environment
Drugs and alcohol provide an easy-to-access method by which to turn down their distress and conceal their struggles

Stimming
Drug use provides intense sensory stimuli
Autistic people often use self-stimulatory behaviours (stimming) to trigger those stimuli repeatedly
We do this because it is enjoyable and helps us regulate our senses and emotions
Some Autistic people report using drugs in this way because the repeated engaging of this sensory experience helps them feel more grounded and able to cope

Community Seeking
Botha (2020) highlights that community-connectedness can reduce the mental health effects of minority stress for Autistic people
Despite this, many Autistic people feel isolated and alone in the world
Drug use can give us access to a social group and shared culture that helps us feel connected to a community

Inpatient Units: Experience and Support

Experience
Inpatient units do not feel like safe spaces
They are unpredictable and high demand
We are unable to effectively co-regulate our emotions with others due to the volatile nature of other inpatients
We spend time forming a new routine, knowing it will be disrupted at some point
For Autistic people in recovery, we face two main challenges
People can be hostile to us for being different
People can be hostile to us if we mention things others do that trigger us
The in-flow of drugs onto psychiatric units can be incredibly difficult, and we can be placed at risk by reporting it to staff

posts.title: Autistic people in inpatient care: Supporting Psychosis and Recovery
posts.text:
Supporting Psychosis and Recovery
The Autistic brain does not care whether an anxious or paranoid thought is factual or accurate, only that it is happening
Trying to disprove an Autistic person’s delusion will likely make them cling onto it tighter, or transfer the paranoia to you
Help the Autistic person logically feel safe
Address the fear without perpetuating the delusion
Find logical solutions to the thing they are worried about to demonstrate they are safe without having to invalidate their experience of reality
