posts.text:
Intersecting Minds: Understanding Psychosis Through a Neurodivergent Lens

Qualified Forensic Scientist
Independent Academic in the field of critical theory, mental health, and neuroqueer theory
Multiply published author
Consultant, mentor, and advocate
Co-founder of Autistic Substance Use Network (ASUN)
Practitioner Member of Addiction Professionals
Professional Member of International Society of Substance Use Professionals (ISSUP)

Why This Conversation Matters
Neurodivergent people are at greater risk of mental health challenges—but the story is more nuanced than pathology.
Families are often left unsure how to respond when a loved one is in distress.
Psychosis presents a significant overlap for Autistic and ADHD people with potential for catastrophic consequences.

What the Research Says
Autistic people are 3–4 times more likely to experience psychosis than non-autistic people.
ADHD is also associated with increased risk, especially when untreated.
Co-occurrence is under-recognised due to diagnostic overshadowing.
Autistic people often report psychotic experiences that are dismissed as "just autism" or “not typical” of psychotic conditions.

Trauma and Neurodivergence
The majority (if not all) of Autistic people have experienced trauma.
Trauma doesn't have to be a singular event – it can be cumulative (e. g. sensory overwhelm, masking, exclusion- not just from violence, accident, or abuse).
Chronic invalidation and gaslighting increase vulnerability to altered states of consciousness as do abuse and conflict.

posts.title: Intersecting Minds: Understanding Psychosis Through a Neurodivergent Lens: Diagnostic Gaps
posts.deck: Intersecting Minds: Understanding Psychosis Through a Neurodivergent Lens
posts.text:
Diagnostic Gaps
Clinicians often lack neurodivergence competence- the ability to learn from and integrate neurodivergent lived experience into thought and practice.
Many are trained to see autism/ADHD and psychosis as mutually exclusive (despite overlapping traits: sensory differences, reality processing, communication styles). Many psychotic diagnoses include a need for distinct separation between autism/ADHD and psychotic features- which is a fundamentally impossible standard to achieve
Disparities in healthcare accessibility for neurodivergent people result in delays with receiving support.
Services are underfunded and lacking in appropriately trained staff.

Psychosis Is Constructed By Experience
Trauma and mistreatment leave neurodivergent people with a lot of distress to process.

Monotropism and Psychosis
Monotropism- The theory that Autistic (and now other neurodivergent people) give more attentional resources to a narrower range of demands.
Monotropic attention (narrow, deep focus) may contribute to perceptual rigidity or hyperfocus on delusional content during distress.
When a monotropic bodymind is overwhelmed, the collapse of cognitive coherence can feel like a break from reality.
This is referred to in community spaces as a monotropic spiral.

posts.title: Intersecting Minds: Understanding Psychosis Through a Neurodivergent Lens: When the World Doesn’t Fit
posts.deck: Intersecting Minds: Understanding Psychosis Through a Neurodivergent Lens
posts.text:
When the World Doesn’t Fit
Psychosis can be a rational reaction to an irrational world—particularly for those forced to mask, code-switch, or endure misunderstanding.
Being “out of sync” with the wider world and constantly needing to adjust how you are seen and perceived takes a huge emotional toll on  neurodivergent people and can create intense identity crises.

What Families Need to Understand

Supporting Through Relationship, Not Control
Co-regulation over confrontation: “Be the calm you want to see.” - If you are unsettled, your loved one will feel less settled.
Non-verbal support can be just as powerful: food, presence, silence, space.
Validate their reality without feeding delusions. We can feel a need to disprove delusions. Sometimes it is better to create a feeling of safety, find logical solutions that honour that what they are experiencing is real for them.

Adjusting Expectations
The goal isn’t to “bring them back to normal.”
The goal is to help them feel safe enough to trust connection again.
Psychosis is a transformative experience. It will change the person experiencing it.
Our goal should be to ensure that the return to shared reality is a positive return, and not one filled with shame and guilt.

Build Neurodivergent Competence
Learn about sensory needs, burnout, communication preferences.
Don’t assume intent behind unusual behaviour—assume unmet need.
Understand that psychosis is a relational and systemic issue, not just a medical one- the power dynamics and relationships in our lives create psychotic experiences just as much as medical issues do.

posts.title: Intersecting Minds: Understanding Psychosis Through a Neurodivergent Lens: Practical Steps for Families
posts.deck: Intersecting Minds: Understanding Psychosis Through a Neurodivergent Lens
posts.text:
Practical Steps for Families

Trauma-Informed Grounding Tools
Familiar and safe sensory items and experiences (weighted blankets, preferred textures, safe foods).
Predictable routines—even in crisis. Loss of routine can create anxiety and a feeling of not being safe
Gentle reorienting away from distressing thoughts and experiences.

Safety Without Escalation
Have a plan with the person when they’re well if they are prone to psychotic experiences.
Seek support from community-based services.
Engage with neurodivergent people to understand the wider experience of neurodivergence.
Use the least restrictive approach possible in that moment.

Self-Care for Supporters
Support doesn’t mean self-erasure.
Your needs matter too.
It is okay to have boundaries and not be able to cope with doing something.
Access peer spaces, online communities, neurodivergent-led trainings.
Healthy support networks increase the chance of a positive rehabilitation experience.

posts.title: Is Autism A Disorder?: A Brief Guide to Language
posts.text:
A Brief Guide to Language
Neurodiversity- The idea that brains and nervous systems are subject to biodiversity
Neurodivergent- A person who can not comfortably perform neurotypical standards
Neurodiverse- A way of describing a group of people that represent multiple neurocognitive styles (Individuals are neurodivergent, groups are neurodiverse)
Neurotypical- A person who can comfortably engage with neuronormative standards of behaviour and cognition
Neuronormativity- The idea that there is a “normal” standard of neurology and cognition that we must all attempt to acheive

A Brief Guide to Language- Community Language Preferences
Survey of 2,750 Autistic community members
69% Identify as Autistic
11. 9% Were unsure if they were Autistic
Remainder were community allies

A Brief Guide to Language- Community Language Preferences
Only 8. 4% preferred person-first language (person with autism) over identity-first (Autistic person) or identity-only (Autistic) language.
77. 6% Did not agree with the use of functioning labels (High functioning/Low functioning autism). The same figure came back as disagreeing with the use of levels to describe autism (Level 1-3 autism)
69. 6% do not agree with the use of aspergers syndrome as a diagnosis
90% did not agree with the use of “Autism Spectrum Disorder” or “Autism Spectrum Condition”

posts.title: Is Autism A Disorder?: Autism as a Disorder: The Historical Context
posts.text:
Autism as a Disorder: The Historical Context
Autism was first overtly described by Leo Kanner in 1943, however it was alluded to prior to this, particularly by Nazi scientists involved in the Aktion T4 project. Kanner described it as ‘Early Infantile Autism’ which while making no solid estimates of prevalence, he believed was rare.
Autistic children have also historically been grouped under Childhood Schizophrenia, which itself evolved out of the previous diagnosis of Dementia Praecox.
The first epidemiological study of autism was conducted in Middlsex by Lotter (1966) and estimated that 4. 5 children in every 10,000 were Autistic

Autism as a Disorder: The Historical Context
Bettelheim (1967) referred to Autistic children as unable to “develop a personality” and blamed emotionally distant mothers for their children’s Autistic experience, this was known as the refrigerator mother theory of autism.
Wing and Gould (1979) went on to introduce the idea of autism as a spectrum, and with this came “the triad of impairments” which were conceptualised as
Impaired Social Interaction
Impaired Communication
Impaired Imagination

posts.title: Is Autism A Disorder?: Autism as a Disorder: The Historical Context
posts.text:
Autism as a Disorder: The Historical Context
By the 1970’s autism had been successfully positioned as a psychopathological condition despite no real understanding of what autism is or how children are born/become Autistic.
During the 1980’s and 90’s Lorna Wing built on the work of Nazi aligned scientist Hans Asperger. Asperger had worked during the second world war to identify gifted disabled children who would be useful to the Nazi war effort while sending those deemed unworthy to the gas chambers.
From this work came the concept of Asperger’s Syndrome, which was essentially autism without language delay or intellectual disability. This term was used diagnostically until 2013 when it was removed from diagnostic manuals and replaced with the broader “Autism Spectrum Disorder”.

Autism as a Disorder: The Historical Context
From Kanners “Classic Autism” through to the contemporary diagnosis of “Autism Spectrum Disorder/Condition”, Autistic people have been positioned as being in deficit, with functional limitations arising from a pathology of the brain rather than barriers placed in their path.
This has set the stage for the collective repression of Autistic people in wider society.

The Pathology Paradigm versus The Neurodiversity Paradigm
Drawing on the work of Dr.
The Pathology Paradigm, arising from the medicalisation of those who can not perform neuronoramtivity
The Neurodiversity Paradigm, Asserting that all brains are unique, and difference in behaviour and cognition is not pathological, but rather the result of natural biodiversity

posts.title: Is Autism A Disorder?: The Pathology Paradigm versus The Neurodiversity Paradigm
posts.text:
The Pathology Paradigm versus The Neurodiversity Paradigm
The pathology paradigm positions autism as a medical diagnosis.
This creates industrial and research efforts to identify and eliminate Autistic brains and beahviour.
The neurodiversity paradigm positions autism primarily as a cultural identity, arguind that Autistic needs and behaviours should be accomodated as opposed to eliminated.
An example of a prior identity that experienced similar framing is homosexuality. This used to be viewed as a psychopathology, but is now widely recognised as a sexuality and identity.

Neuronormativity and the Medicalisation of Autism
The pathology paradigm operates on the concept that there is a correct standard of behaviour and cognition. It is rooted in the concept of “The Average Man” as described by Quetelet in the 1800’s. This concept of average became targeted in favour of those who could benefit the capitalist system.
This coupled with Cartesian Models of health that viewed deviation from “average” as functioning incorrectly, and ultimately gave rise to the eugenics work of Francis Galton starting around 1883. Galton was the cousin of Charles Darwin and believed the human race could be improved by eliminating undesirable traits from the populace.

posts.title: Is Autism A Disorder?: Neuronormativity and the Medicalisation of Autism
posts.text:
Neuronormativity and the Medicalisation of Autism
This view of autism and other neurocognitive styles as a set of undesirable traits laid the framework for the medicalisation of autism, with many Autistic people being locked away in institutions. Sadly, this practice is still happening to this day.
In contemporary times, the medicalisation of autism has created harmful behavioural interventions such as Applied Beahviour Analysis (ABA) and Positive Behaviour Support (PBS) that aim to teach neuronormative standards of behaviour through operant conditioning.
There is also extensive research into medical interventions for autism such as pre-natal testing, and pharmaceutical treatment of autism.

The Implications of Viewing Autism as a Disorder
This pathological view of autism has not only resulted in behavioural interventions and ethically sanctioned research.
It has also created clandestine industries of fake cures such as MMS (feeding bleach to Autistic children), Chelation Therapy (Using drugs to strip heavy metal from the body), and Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy (the use of high pressure compartments to cure autism).
Further to this, it has bolstered the idea that Autistic people are somwhat less human than non-Autistic people, justifying their exclusion and mistreatment, and the systemic discrimination and oppression of those with this neurocognitive style.

posts.title: Is Autism A Disorder?: The Neurodiversity Movement as a Civil Rights Movement
posts.text:
The Neurodiversity Movement as a Civil Rights Movement
The neurodiversity movement evolved out of an online forum in the 1990’s called “Independent Living” (INLV). The term is often falsely attributed to Judy Singer, but while she may have been the first to use the term academically, their is strong evidence that “neurodiversity” was being discussed in INLV communities prior to her work.
The neurodiversity movement, in line with the similarly named paradigm, evolved out of a desire to end the over-medicalisation and oppression of neurodivergent people. While it is often associated with Autistic rights, the neurodiversity movement fights for the demedicalisation of a astoundingly wide array of neurocognitive styles.

The Neurodiversity Movement as a Civil Rights Movement
The neurodiversity movement essentially rests on one key idea-
Neurodivergent people should not be at a disadvantage purely because their neurology differs from the assumed “average” neurology.

posts.title: Is Autism A Disorder?: Autistic People as a Cultural Identity Group
posts.text:
Autistic People as a Cultural Identity Group
The idea of Autistic people being a cultural group is widely accepted in Autistic online spaces
Further to this, the work of Botha et al (2022) reported Autistic people highlighting a feeling of community connectedness across multiple facets of experience, including wellbeing and political views
Milton (2012) discusses how differing cultural experiences result in a empathy divide between Autistic and non-Autistic groups and individuals. This idea is widely supported in Autistic spaces, and could not function as a theory without a differing cultural experience between the two groups

Autistic People as a Cultural Identity Group
They have no entry or exit point, they are interdependent, but the removal of one point in the community will not necessarily threaten the others. Community spaces are interest-led, with participation driven by intrinsic motivation rather than compliance with hierarchy

Is Autism a Disability
Many assume that if autism is not viewed as a disorder then it also can not be viewed as a disability. This is a false equivalance.
The neurodiversity movement upholds the social model of disability. In this respect, the functional limitations of an Autistic person become disabling due to systemic and environmental barriers and lack of accessibility rather than medical pathology
In this respect, the disability of Autistic people is seen more as a result of oppression and discrimination
Furthermore, the Autistic community stands largely opposed to the pejoration of disabled identity

posts.title: Is Autism A Disorder?: The Importance of Community to Autistic People
posts.text:
The Importance of Community to Autistic People
Additional work by Both and colleagues has indicated that community connectedness reduces the impact of minority stress on Autistic people.
Minority stress can be understood as the cumulative stress that marginalised groups experience via their stgmatisation and discrimination.
Research has indicated that Being part of the Autistic community improves wellbeing and mental health outcomes for Autistic people, further upholding the importance of moving away from the idea of autism as a disorder

Creating a Neurocosmopolitan Society
Neurocosmopolitanism is an idea proposed by Dr.
She conceptualised a neurocosmopolitan society as a place where no neurocognitive style has privilege or preference over another
Such a society would afford equal access and support to all people, and not lock support behind diagnostic pathways and medical assessments
The first step to a neurcosmopolitan society is to shift mainstream attitudes towards an understanding that all humans have unique and dynamic needs and neurocognitive styles, and away from the idea of “expected” or “normal” embodiment of the Self
While the competing needs of individuals present a challenge to future scholars working towards the realisation of such a society, we can start the work today by moving away from the medicalisation of human experience, and liberating the oppressed culture of Autistic people

Living Between Lilipads:
Supporting Flow, Connection, and Recovery

What Lilipadding means

The Problem We’re Trying To Solve
Many neurodivergent people live adapted lives; surviving, not thriving
Expectations to be consistent or linear cause burnout and shame
Parents and carers are often told to “fix” rather than understand
We need a framework that celebrates fluidity, authenticity, and rest

What Is Lilipadding?

Understanding The Concept
Every moment in our life is a transition; room to room, activity to activity, breath to breath
Lilipadding is a conceptual framework through which we can understand and navigate these transitions
A metaphor for how neurodivergent people move through life authentically
Each “lilypad” represents a state, focus, or part of identity; work, rest, creativity, relationships
It’s about moving fluidly between these lilipads instead of forcing yourself to stay on one
A way of honouring your current capacity rather than fighting it

posts.title: Lilipadding 30min: The Practical Application Of Lilipadding
posts.text:
The Practical Application Of Lilipadding
Transitions aren’t hard because we’re Neurodivergent; they’re hard when they’re enforced in hostile or unpredictable environments.
Lilipadding is a relational, co-constructed practice that honours monotropic attention and supports movement without rupture.
It’s not a compliance tool; it’s consent-based pacing that bridges states of focus and readiness.
Flow is sacred: Lilipadding protects continuity rather than breaking it.
It replaces timers and demands with attunement, collaboration, and sensory safety.
Each Lilypad is a stepping stone, designed with the person, not at them.

The Lilipad As A Metaphor
The pond = your whole life
Lilypads = places of safety, focus, or belonging
Water = uncertainty, transition, reflection
Movement between pads = growth, change, and self-alignment

Lilipadding As A Parent/Carer
You have Lilipads too: your routines, coping spaces, passions
Understanding your own transitions models authenticity
It’s okay to move gently between roles; parent, advocate, individual
Supporting them starts with supporting your own rhythm

posts.title: Neuronormativity: What is it:: Neuronormativity: What is it?
posts.text:
Neuronormativity: What is it?

Learning Objectives
Understand what neuronormativity is
Consider how neuronormativity effects Autistic people
Discuss how neuronormativity informs the Autistic sense of identity
Think about how we might oppose neuronormativity

What is neuronormativity?
Neuronormativity is the belief and enforcement of a standard expression of ones neurology.
Similar to heteronormativity, it is used as the basis of a world that values assimilation over diversity.

What is neuronormativity?
Neuronormativity takes many forms:
Forced conversion and assimilation using techniques such as Applied Behavioural Analysis
Creating environments that have specific standards of behaviour and self-expression
Forced medication in order to get a person to comply with standardised expression of self

How does neuronormativity harm
Autistic people?
Many Autistic people are exposed to so-called ‘therapies’ that aim to make them “indistinguishable from their peers”.
This forced assimilation does not change the persons neurology, they are still Autistic.
What it teaches them is to mask in order to assimilate.

What is masking?
Masking is a survival mechanism.
Contrary to popular belief, it is not a choice.
We use various techniques to appear more neurotypical, in order to keep ourselves safe from discrimination and harm.

How do we combat neuronormativity?
There is a vital theory that teaches us about authentic expression of the Self.
It is known as Neuroqueer theory.

posts.title: Neuronormativity: What is it:: Who conceptualised Neuroqueer
posts.text:
Who conceptualised Neuroqueer
theory?
The person who is best known for conceptualising Neuroqueer theory is Dr.
She is a Trans and Autistic academic from california.

What is Neuroqueer theory?
Neuroqueer theory was adopted out of Queer theory.
It posits that one can queer the expectations of societal neuronormativity.
This can be achieved in a number of ways, including:
Authentic expression of neurodivergent behaviour
Queering of gender and sexual expectations that is inherently linked to ones neurology
Using psychedelic drugs to alter one's own neurology
The use of meditation techniques to alter one's neurology

How does neuroqueer theory apply to
You are Neuroqueer, if you neuroqueer
By queering the expectations placed on the way one expresses their neurology, you are neuroqueering
Neuroqueerness can also be seen in people who have divergent gender and sexual identities that are intrinsically linked to their neurology.

How does this apply to
neuronnormativity?
You can’t unqueer a queer mind, only queer it further
You can’t take an Autistic person and ‘remove’ the autism
All you will do is traumatise them, furthering their neurodivergence

Does this only apply to autism?
No.
Neurodivergence can be found both intrinsically, and acquired.
An Autistic person is just as neurodivergent as a Schizophrenic person.
One is innate, the other acquired through traumatic experiences.
Neuronormativity hurts every Neurodivergent person.
Trying to force a person’s assimilation can lead to further acquired neurodivergence.
Neuroqueer expression can apply to anyone trying to subvert expectations.

Is Autism A Spectrum?

Uta Frith's Argument
Uta Frith contends that autism lacks a unified defining characteristic across those diagnosed. She perceives the spectrum's diversity as a sign of excessive expansion, advocating for a return to narrower categories like Asperger's syndrome and childhood autism.

Variable Neurocognition
Neurocognition varies widely among individuals, reflecting diverse sensory processing, cognition, personality, and learning styles. Autism illustrates these distributed differences rather than conforming to a single biological pathway.
Spectrum Model

Neurological Diversity
Understanding The Nature Of Autism

Rising Diagnoses

Psychiatric Patient
Two admissions to a psychiatric inpatient facility
Exposed to drug and alcohol use on the ward

Psychiatry’s Historical Context

Pathologisation Of Autistic Experience
Psychiatry operates from an assumption that the medical model of disability is the “correct” way to view autism and mental health
This pathologisation of neurodivergence has shaped diagnostic criteria
It has shaped the history of psychological and sociological inquiry into neurodivergence
This is problematic for not just Autistic people in general, but the countless Autistic people who experience mental health concerns (Lai et al, 2019)

Accessing Psychiatry

posts.title: Psychiatric Power Autistic Presentation: Gatekeeping & Control In Modern Psychiatry
posts.text:
Gatekeeping & Control In Modern Psychiatry
Biased research and systemic under-resourcing has resulted in issue with accessing diagnosis and support
Minority groups struggle to get an autism diagnosis, and Autistic people in general are more likely to receive a psychiatric disordder diagnosis
Despite this, many western countries are facing a crisis in which those who need psychiatric support are either left to fend for themselves, or have their liberty restricted
Psychiatrists are positioned as having power over Autistic people when they seek support, with Autistic people not only having to fight for access, but then fight to have a voice in their treatment
Many Autistic people are faced with complying with medication and therapy regimes that do not help them (Weston et al, 2016) or risk being ejected from the psychiatric system altogether

Autistic Identity & Wellbeing

The Impact
Autistic people are forced to abandon their identity and instead take on the new identity of “patient” (Botha et al, 2021)
This further unbalances the power imbalance between Autistic people and the psychiatric system
We are told that to be Autistic is a “disorder” and that we should not allow it to be part of our identity
This denies us  access to our communities and therefore denies us access to our wellbeing
Research has shown us that community connectedness has a positive impact on the wellbeing effects of minority stress (Botha, 2020)
The psychiatric system prevents that improvement by pathologising our existence and mental health

Reclaiming Our Identities

posts.title: Qualitative SU: Improving substance use services for autistic adults: Insights and recommendations from autistic adults
posts.text:
Improving substance use services for autistic adults: Insights and recommendations from autistic adults
Munday et al.
Autistic Substance Use Network

Why Did We Research This?
We undertook this research because autistic people are at higher risk of harmful substance use yet face services designed without their realities in mind.
Existing addiction frameworks and clinical models often misunderstand autistic embodiment, ignore trauma and sensory needs, and apply one-size-fits-all approaches that create barriers to care.

What Did We Hope To Achieve?
We hoped to centre autistic people’s lived experiences to expose the barriers they face in substance use services and show how current models fail to meet their needs.
By doing so, we aimed to guide the creation of accessible, trauma-informed, and neurodivergent-competent care that genuinely supports autistic substance users.

How Did We Do This Research?
475 Participants
Online One-Time Cross-Sectional Questionnaire
Designed In Co-Creation With Autistic People
Characteristics
Autistic Adults
Aged 18+
Formally or Self-Identified
Reported Current Or Prior Substance Use
87. 36% Reported Anxiety
75. 16% Reported Depression
80. 42% Co-Occurring ADHD

Service Accessibility & Competence
Participants spoke about accessibility issues when they accessed (or tried to access) substance use services. Several participants shared that the service providers lacked a choice of communication methods and that group sessions were particularly inaccessible.

posts.title: Qualitative SU: Inadequate Professional Knowledge And Understanding
posts.text:
Inadequate Professional Knowledge And Understanding
Participants experienced professionals who had a limited understanding of substance use and autistic embodiment (how autistic people interact with and make sense of the world). Some participants described having experienced inadequate care, whilst others were worried about accessing substance use services due to this perceived lack of knowledge.

Reducing Harm Through Trauma-Informed, Neuro-Affirming Practice
Participants suggested that substance use services should focus on harm reduction through taking a trauma-informed approach which reduces shame and stigma associated with substance use.

Recommendations
Services should be redesigned to be sensory-friendly, flexible, and easier to navigate, offering options like quiet spaces, video sessions, and one-to-one or autistic-specific support instead of defaulting to group work.
Professionals need regular, autistic-led training on communication styles, sensory profiles, and why autistic people may use substances, including interoception support to help clients understand their own bodies.
Care should move beyond abstinence-only models toward harm reduction and trauma-informed, neurodivergent-competent approaches, with autistic people involved in shaping and delivering services and staff training

posts.title: Six Point Framework: NeuroHub Community Ltd — Supporting Autistic People: A Six-Point Framework
posts.text:
NeuroHub Community Ltd — Supporting Autistic People: A Six-Point Framework
01 — UNDERSTANDING AUTISTIC EXPERIENCE
Understanding Autistic Experience
Autism is not a list of behaviours; it is a world.
Autistic experience is shaped by a different rhythm of attention, communication, sensory processing, and identity.
Support begins with understanding that world on its own terms.
• Monotropism — deep attentional focus; transitions are harder, immersion is easier
• Double Empathy Problem — communication breakdowns are mutual; Autistic communication is often
clearer and more direct
• The Chaotic Self — identity shifts continuously in response to context; this is adaptation, not instability
• When we see Autistic people through their own worldview, support becomes connection rather than
correction
REFLECTIVE PROMPT
02 — THE SENSORY & EMOTIONAL LANDSCAPE
The Sensory & Emotional Landscape
Autistic wellbeing begins with the bodymind.
Autistic people navigate an eight-sense world — including proprioception, vestibular processing, and
interoception. These shape how the body experiences safety, overwhelm, and regulation.
• Sensory overload is a physical crisis, not misbehaviour
• Stimming is self-regulation — it should be supported, not suppressed
• Retreating and nesting are valid and necessary self-care
• Meltdowns and shutdowns are overwhelmed nervous systems, not choices
• When environments respect sensory needs, Autistic people gain stability, confidence, and emotional safety
REFLECTIVE PROMPT
What does the sensory environment here ask of this person, and is that ask reasonable?

posts.title: Six Point Framework: NeuroHub Community Ltd — Supporting Autistic People: A Six-Point Framework
posts.text:
NeuroHub Community Ltd — Supporting Autistic People: A Six-Point Framework
03 — AUTISTIC BURNOUT: A CRISIS OF CONNECTION
Autistic Burnout: A Crisis of Connection
Burnout is a total collapse — not a bad week.
Burnout emerges when demands exceed capacity for too long. It is ecosystemic — shaped by environments,
expectations, and systemic pressures — not personal failure.
• Signs include: loss of skills, executive dysfunction, intense exhaustion, and withdrawal from life or
relationships
• Recovery requires reconnection: to the body, to routine, to community, and to Autistic identity
• Burnout is caused by systems, not by the individual — our role is to reduce demands, not increase them
• Early recognition is one of the most important skills in this work
REFLECTIVE PROMPT
Are the demands being placed on this person sustainable? What could we reduce?
04 — IDENTITY, LANGUAGE & DISABILITY MODELS
Identity, Language & Disability Models
Autistic identity is personhood.
Most Autistic people prefer identity-first language (‘Autistic person’) because autism is not separate from who
they are. NeuroHub uses identity-first language throughout all our work.
• Diagnosis should never gatekeep identity — self-identification is valid
• Functioning labels are harmful and inaccurate; avoid ‘high-functioning’ and ‘low-functioning’
• The social model of disability offers a more accurate understanding than deficit frameworks
• Neurodivergence must be understood relationally, not as individual deficit
• Supporting Autistic identity builds confidence, resilience, and wellbeing
REFLECTIVE PROMPT
Is our language building this person’s sense of identity and belonging, or undermining it?

posts.title: Six Point Framework: NeuroHub Community Ltd — Supporting Autistic People: A Six-Point Framework
posts.text:
NeuroHub Community Ltd — Supporting Autistic People: A Six-Point Framework
05 — TRAUMA, SAFETY & THE EMOTIONAL ENVIRONMENT
Trauma, Safety & the Emotional Environment
Safety is the foundation of every Autistic life.
Autistic trauma is often sensory and relational rather than event-based. It arises from chronic overload,
communication invalidation, masking, coercive ‘support’, and pressure to perform neurotypicality.
• Trauma-informed support requires predictability, sensory safety, and genuine autonomy
• Co-regulation, acceptance of rest and retreat, and non-punitive boundaries are essential
• Coercive ‘support’ — including compliance-based approaches — causes harm
• A safe Autistic person is a connected, expressive, and resilient Autistic person
REFLECTIVE PROMPT
Does this person experience our environment as genuinely safe — and if not, what would
change that?
06 — LEARNING FROM AUTISTIC COMMUNITY
Learning From Autistic Community
Autistic people understand Autistic life best.
Autistic community is a vital source of knowledge, belonging, and cultural identity. Professionals who learn from
Autistic voices become genuinely neurodivergence-competent.
• Lived-experience wisdom should shape and inform our practice
• Autistic cultural norms — sensory-friendly spaces, direct communication, humour, solidarity — are valid and
valuable
• Strategies that come from Autistic community actually work
• Autistic community is not optional; it is transformative
REFLECTIVE PROMPT
Whose voices are informing our approach? Are we learning from Autistic people themselves?
Why this framework matters
Autistic people do not thrive through compliance, behavioural control, or trying to ‘fit in’. Autistic people thrive
through connection, safety, autonomy, sensory respect, positive identity, community, and belonging. This
framework gives everyone supporting Autistic people — professionals, educators, clinicians, families — the tools to
build environments where Autistic lives can flourish.
Autism is not something people grow out of.
It is something people grow into.

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar 2: What Is a Spiky Profile?
posts.text:
What Is a Spiky Profile?
Section 1 — Spiky Profiles
High peaks and deep troughs
Autistic cognitive profiles show far greater variation between strengths and difficulties than neurotypical profiles.
Not inconsistency — architecture
A person highly capable in verbal reasoning may find processing speed tasks genuinely difficult. These co-exist; neither cancels the other.
Scatter in assessment
Subtest scatter is significantly higher in Autistic assessments. This is diagnostically meaningful and should inform all support planning.
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org
(Speaker notes: The spiky profile concept describes the characteristically uneven distribution of cognitive strengths and difficulties in Autistic people. This is not inconsistency or effort — it is the genuine shape of how the Autistic mind works.)

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar 2: The Myth of the Global Deficit
posts.text:
The Myth of the Global Deficit
Section 1 — Spiky Profiles
The 'global deficit' framing assumes difficulty in one area predicts difficulty across all — this does not hold for Autistic people
'But they can do X, so they must be able to do Y' — this reasoning is consistently wrong and consistently harmful
An Autistic person with exceptional memory may have profound difficulties with processing speed — both are real and simultaneous
Social and communicative difficulties do not imply intellectual limitations; intellectual capacity does not imply ease with sensory or executive demands
Spiky profiles mean that functioning in one context tells you very little about functioning in a different one
Good support starts from the actual profile — not an assumed hierarchy of ability
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

Spiky Profiles in Practice
Section 1 — Spiky Profiles
Always map the full profile — peaks and troughs — rather than averaging toward a 'level'
Do not use performance in a high-support, low-demand context as evidence that high-support is no longer needed
Adjustments addressing one area of the profile do not automatically transfer to other areas
Autistic people are not inconsistent when they perform well in one domain and struggle in another on the same day
Fatigue and load shift the profile — a person's best performance in assessment conditions may not represent their daily functional capacity
Ask: what specifically is difficult here, and what specifically is the demand — not 'how able is this person overall?'
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar 2: Monotropism
posts.text:
Monotropism
A theory of Autistic cognition grounded in the interest system

The Monotropic Mind
Murray, Lesser & Lawson (2005) — attention, interest, and the shape of Autistic cognition
→
FOCUS
Deep resource
allocated here
Many inputs in the environment
Interest system
Autistic people have a powerful interest system — things within the tunnel of attention receive rich, sustained, resourced engagement.
Outside the tunnel
Tasks and demands outside the current area of focus receive comparatively little resource — not due to laziness or refusal, but to attentional architecture.
Depth over breadth
The monotropic advantage is extraordinary depth: pattern recognition, expertise, sustained output in areas of focus that polytropic minds rarely achieve.
The cost of switching
Pulling attention from a monotropic focus requires the nervous system to disengage and reallocate — a genuinely costly process, not a preference.
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org
(Speaker notes: Monotropism proposes that Autistic people's interest and attention system is organised around fewer, deeper areas of focus at any one time. The analogy is a spotlight versus a floodlight — monotropic attention is intense and narrow, polytropic attention is broad and distributed.)

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar 2: Special Interests and Monotropic Flow
posts.text:
Special Interests and Monotropic Flow
Section 2 — Monotropism
Special interests as resource
Special interests generate genuine joy, competence, and identity
Monotropic flow states produce exceptional depth of output
Interests provide reliable regulation — they are not frivolous
Connection through shared interests is a genuine relational pathway for many Autistic people
Restricting or pathologising interests removes a major source of wellbeing
How interests get misread
Described as 'obsessions' — pathologising language that frames a strength as a symptom
Used as rewards or withheld as punishment — treating regulation as a bargaining chip
'They only talk about one thing' — monotropic communication is depth-focused, not deficient
Transitions away from interests treated as non-compliance rather than nervous system demand
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org
(Speaker notes: The concept of special interests is central to Autistic experience and to monotropism. They are not a symptom to be managed — they are a primary source of wellbeing, regulation, identity, and connection.)

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar 2: Transitions as Genuine Demand
posts.text:
Transitions as Genuine Demand
Section 2 — Monotropism
From a monotropic perspective, every transition requires the nervous system to disengage from one attentional focus and re-engage with another — this is a real cognitive and neurological cost
The demand is not proportional to how important the transition seems to the observer — it is proportional to the depth of the current monotropic engagement
Transition difficulty is not defiance, rigidity, or manipulation — it is a predictable feature of monotropic attentional architecture
Predictable transitions with advance warning are significantly easier than sudden demands to switch
Timers, visual schedules, and verbal pre-warnings reduce transition demand — not because they trick the person but because they allow the nervous system to begin disengaging before the demand arrives
The five-minute warning is not a courtesy — it is a neurological accommodation
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

The Double Empathy Problem
Rethinking where communication breakdown actually lies

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar 2: From Deficit to Dialogue
posts.text:
From Deficit to Dialogue
Dr Damian Milton (2012) — reconsidering the framing of Autistic communication
The old framing
Theory of mind deficit — Autistic people cannot understand others have different mental states
Mindblindness (Baron-Cohen) — Autistic people structurally unable to empathise
Communication difficulty located entirely within the Autistic person
Non-Autistic people's difficulty understanding Autistic people goes completely unexamined
The Double Empathy Problem
Communication breakdown between Autistic and non-Autistic people is mutual — not one-directional
Non-Autistic people also fail to understand Autistic people — and this has been treated as unproblematic
Autistic people communicate well with other Autistic people — disproving the deficit claim
The 'problem' is in the cross-neurotype interaction, not in either party individually
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org
(Speaker notes: The theory of mind deficit and mindblindness framings have been enormously influential and enormously harmful. They positioned Autistic people as fundamentally unable to relate to others — a claim now substantially undermined by research.)

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar 2: What the Research Shows
posts.text:
What the Research Shows
Section 3 — Double Empathy Problem
Crompton et al. (2020)
Autistic people shared information just as well with other Autistic people as non-Autistic people did with each other. Cross-neurotype dyads showed reduced transmission fidelity on both sides.
Cook et al. (2021)
Non-Autistic people formed more negative first impressions of Autistic people within seconds — without any diagnostic information. This bias was not reciprocated by Autistic people toward non-Autistic people.
Sasson et al. (2017)
Non-Autistic observers rated Autistic people as less likeable, less trustworthy, and less attractive for friendship after brief interactions — the deficit in the interaction is not located where the clinical literature assumed.
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org
(Speaker notes: The research base for the double empathy problem is now substantial. The key findings consistently point in the same direction: communication difficulties in cross-neurotype interactions are bidirectional, and negative social judgements of Autistic people arise from non-Autistic bias, not Autistic deficit.)

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar 2: Implications for Practice
posts.text:
Implications for Practice
Section 3 — Double Empathy Problem
When you find it hard to understand an Autistic person, do not locate that difficulty in the Autistic person — it belongs to the interaction
First impressions of Autistic people are systematically biased by non-Autistic expectations of social presentation — be aware of this in assessment and referral contexts
Autistic communication styles (directness, literal language, different eye contact, different body language) are not failures — they are a different but coherent communicative system
Bridging the communication gap is a shared responsibility; adapting your communication to an Autistic person's style is a professional skill, not an accommodation granted by goodwill
Creating Autistic-to-Autistic peer connection opportunities is therapeutically meaningful — it is not a consolation prize for failed socialisation
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

Energy Accounting
The finite resource of existing as an Autistic person in a neurotypical world

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar 2: What Is Energy Accounting?
posts.text:
What Is Energy Accounting?
Section 4 — Energy Accounting
Energy accounting treats cognitive, sensory, and emotional energy as a finite resource — with income (restoration) and outgoings (demand) that must be understood and balanced.
The baseline difference
Navigating a neurotypical world costs Autistic people significantly more energy than it costs non-Autistic people — before any specific task begins.
Tasks that are hidden costs
Masking, sensory filtering, social translation, transition, interoceptive monitoring, and executive function all consume energy invisibly — they are not visible to observers.
The budget can run out
When outgoings exceed income consistently, the result is depletion — which may present as shutdown, burnout, meltdown, or withdrawal. The person has not 'given up'; they are out of resource.
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org
(Speaker notes: Energy accounting is a practical framework developed in Autistic communities — building on but going beyond spoon theory — to describe the finite nature of the resources Autistic people bring to daily life.)

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar 2: The Energy Budget
posts.text:
The Energy Budget
Section 4 — Energy Accounting
OUTGOINGS — What depletes energy
Masking and camouflaging Autistic traits
Sensory filtering in overwhelming environments
Social translation — decoding implicit communication
Unplanned transitions and changes to routine
Interoceptive monitoring (identifying hunger, pain, emotion)
Executive function tasks: planning, initiation, switching
Recovery from meltdown or shutdown
Healthcare and service appointments
INCOME — What restores energy
Time with special interests and monotropic flow
Solitude and low-sensory environments
Predictable routine with no unexpected demands
Stimming without suppression
Connection with other Autistic people
Being genuinely understood — no performance required
Rest that is genuine rest, not just inactivity
Physical safety and psychological safety
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org
(Speaker notes: Good energy accounting support involves understanding both columns — not just reducing demands but actively protecting and building recovery. Many Autistic people have been conditioned to minimise their income column, especially around special interests.)

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar 2: Energy Accounting in Practice
posts.text:
Energy Accounting in Practice
Section 4 — Energy Accounting
End-of-day depletion is not a sign that the Autistic person cannot manage — it is a sign that their energy budget has been spent, often largely on hidden costs
Do not measure an Autistic person's capacity by their performance at the end of a high-demand day
Planning support means mapping the energy cost of a day — not just its tasks — and building in genuine recovery
Forcing continuation after depletion does not build capacity — it deepens the deficit and risks burnout
Protect the income column: special interests, solitude, stimming, and predictability are not indulgences but essential energy sources
Ask: what has this person's energy budget already been spent on today, before they arrived here?
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

Minority Stress
The chronic health burden of social marginalisation

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar 2: The Minority Stress Model
posts.text:
The Minority Stress Model
Meyer (2003), extended to Autistic populations by Botha et al. — social context as a determinant of Autistic mental health
SOCIAL CONTEXT: Being part of a stigmatised neurological minority in a neurotypical-normative world
↓
↓
DISTAL STRESSORS
External events: discrimination, victimisation, prejudice, exclusion, microaggressions, systems failures
PROXIMAL STRESSORS
Internal processes: expectation of rejection, concealment of identity, internalised stigma, hypervigilance
↓
OUTCOMES: Elevated rates of anxiety, depression, suicidality, self-harm, PTSD, and other mental health difficulties — located in social context, not in Autism itself
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org
(Speaker notes: The minority stress model was developed by Ilan Meyer to explain the elevated rates of mental health difficulties in LGB populations — difficulties that could not be explained by any inherent feature of LGB identity, only by the experience of being a stigmatised minority. Botha and colleagues have extended and validated this model for Autistic populations.)

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar 2: Minority Stress and Autistic People
posts.text:
Minority Stress and Autistic People
Section 5 — Minority Stress
Autistic people experience significantly elevated rates of anxiety, depression, suicidality, and self-harm compared to the general population — this is well-evidenced
Minority stress locates these elevated rates in the social experience of being Autistic, not in Autism itself — this is a crucial distinction for how support is designed
Concealment and masking are proximal stressors: the cost of hiding one's neurotype to avoid rejection compounds the impact of the rejection itself
Internalised stigma — absorbing negative cultural messages about Autism — is a proximal stressor that late-diagnosed adults frequently carry unexamined
Discrimination, victimisation, and social exclusion are distal stressors that accumulate across the lifetime
Neurodiversity-affirming environments and Autistic community connection function as buffers against minority stress — they are protective factors, not optional extras
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

Vulnerability to Violence & Exploitation
The elevated risk Autistic people face — and what it requires of practitioners

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar 2: The Scale of the Problem
posts.text:
The Scale of the Problem
Section 6 — Vulnerability to Violence & Exploitation
3–4×
more likely to experience sexual abuse than non-Autistic people (Haruvi-Lamdan et al. , 2021)
8×
higher rates of physical victimisation in childhood (Zeedyk et al. , 2014)
2–3×
higher lifetime rates of domestic violence and intimate partner violence
~40%
of Autistic adults report having been bullied in the workplace (NAS, UK)
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org
(Speaker notes: These are not marginal statistics. Autistic people — and particularly Autistic women, girls, and people with co-occurring learning disabilities — face dramatically elevated rates of abuse and exploitation. This is a safeguarding issue as much as a clinical one.)

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar 2: Structural Risk Factors
posts.text:
Structural Risk Factors
Section 6 — Vulnerability to Violence & Exploitation — risk is structural, not naivety
Risk is not a character failing — it arises from the intersection of Autistic neurological profile with environments that are frequently unsafe, and support systems that have failed to provide adequate protection.
Difficulty identifying and responding to implicit threat cues — danger is often communicated indirectly, which Autistic people may not read as intended
Elevated trust in authority figures and people presenting as helpful — exploiters actively target this
Mate crime: predatory befriending of Autistic people specifically to gain access, resources, or to exploit
Social isolation and limited peer network — fewer people in the person's life who might notice warning signs
Dependency on support systems — where abusers may hold positions of authority or trust
Previous trauma histories increase vulnerability to re-exploitation
Difficulty being believed — Autistic people's accounts are frequently disbelieved or misinterpreted in disclosure contexts
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org
(Speaker notes: The framing of 'naivety' as the primary risk factor is both inaccurate and harmful — it individualises a structural problem. The risk is produced by environments that are not designed to protect Autistic people, and by predators who specifically target Autistic people.)

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar 2: Mate Crime and Grooming
posts.text:
Mate Crime and Grooming
Section 6 — Vulnerability to Violence & Exploitation
What is mate crime?
Mate crime describes the targeting of a person by someone presenting as a friend — with the intention of exploiting them financially, sexually, or otherwise. Autistic people's desire for friendship and social connection is specifically targeted.
Grooming patterns
Perpetrators offer friendship, gifts, and belonging — meeting needs that Autistic people may have struggled to have met elsewhere. The exploitation follows once trust is established and social isolation from other relationships has occurred.
Financial exploitation
Access to resources, accommodation, and benefits is a common target. Autistic people may not recognise financial exploitation or may find it very difficult to set limits on people they perceive as friends.
Online contexts
Online spaces are both important social environments for Autistic people and contexts of elevated risk. The absence of non-verbal cues can reduce already-limited access to threat recognition — while providing a low-effort access route for perpetrators.
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org
(Speaker notes: Mate crime is a specific and well-documented form of exploitation targeting neurodivergent and learning-disabled people. Practitioners need to be alert to patterns of befriending, and to support Autistic people to understand healthy versus exploitative relationships — without catastrophising all social connection.)

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar 2: Safeguarding Implications for Practitioners
posts.text:
Safeguarding Implications for Practitioners
Section 6 — Vulnerability to Violence & Exploitation
Maintain a heightened safeguarding awareness with all Autistic people — this is not optional additional practice, it is a core professional responsibility
Take disclosures seriously: Autistic people are more likely to be disbelieved; be aware of this bias in yourself and in systems
Teach relationship skills in terms of genuine rights, limits, and reciprocity — not scripts that can be easily manipulated
Be aware of dependency dynamics in your own professional relationship — practitioners and services can also be sites of exploitation and coercion
Create regular, low-pressure opportunities for Autistic people to disclose concerns — many will not initiate disclosure without an explicit opening
Understand that the goal of safeguarding is not to restrict Autistic people's social lives but to ensure those lives are genuinely safer
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

Co-occurring Conditions
Understanding what frequently accompanies Autism — and why it matters for support

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar 2: Mental Health Co-occurrences
posts.text:
Mental Health Co-occurrences
Section 7 — Co-occurring Conditions — frequently present alongside Autism, often unrecognised
Anxiety Disorders
~40–50%
Including GAD, social anxiety, and specific phobias. Often presents differently — may not include typical worry cognitions.
Depression
~35–50%
Frequently co-occurs with burnout and is often secondary to years of masking, rejection, and unmet needs.
OCD
~17–37%
Repetitive behaviours in OCD and Autism are phenomenologically distinct — conflating them leads to inappropriate treatment.
PTSD / Complex Trauma
~20–35%+
Elevated due to childhood adversity, bullying, harmful interventions, and medical trauma. May not present with classic PTSD features.
Eating Disorders
~20–35%
Including ARFID (Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder), anorexia, and atypical presentations strongly linked to sensory profile and demand profile.
Suicidality
Significantly elevated
Autistic people face dramatically elevated rates of suicidal ideation and attempt. Minority stress, masking, and late diagnosis are key drivers.
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org
(Speaker notes: Prevalence figures should be taken as indicative rather than definitive — research methodologies vary and the true rates are likely higher given diagnostic overshadowing. The key point is that these are not rare co-occurrences: they are the norm, not the exception.)

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar 2: Neurodevelopmental & Physical Co-occurrences
posts.text:
Neurodevelopmental & Physical Co-occurrences
Section 7 — Co-occurring Conditions
ADHD
50–70%
The most common co-occurrence. Shared and distinct features require careful differentiation. Executive function difficulties compound for both.
Dyslexia / Dyspraxia / Dyscalculia
Significantly elevated
Overlapping neurodevelopmental profiles are common. Dyspraxia (DCD) affects motor coordination and is frequently unidentified in Autistic people.
PDA Profile
Subgroup within Autism
Persistent/Pathological Demand Avoidance — or Pervasive Drive for Autonomy. A distinct Autistic profile requiring very different support approaches to standard Autism practice.
Hypermobility / EDS
Significantly elevated
Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome and Hypermobility Spectrum Disorders co-occur at elevated rates. Joint pain, fatigue, and proprioceptive differences compound sensory profile.
Epilepsy
~20–30%
Particularly in Autistic people with intellectual disability. Medication interactions and seizure presentations need careful monitoring.
GI Issues & Sleep Disorders
Very common
Gastrointestinal problems and sleep difficulties affect a high proportion of Autistic people and significantly impact on daily functioning and mental health.
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org
(Speaker notes: The physical co-occurrences are frequently overlooked in autism-focused practice. EDS/HSD in particular is substantially under-recognised in Autistic people, despite strong research evidence of co-occurrence. Physical pain and fatigue significantly amplify the energy accounting challenges described earlier.)

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar 2: Implications for Assessment and Support
posts.text:
Implications for Assessment and Support
Section 7 — Co-occurring Conditions
Co-occurring conditions are the norm in Autistic populations — assessment that looks only for Autism will routinely miss what is also present
Diagnostic overshadowing: attributing all symptoms to Autism may mean co-occurring conditions go untreated
ADHD and Autism together require support that addresses both profiles — each changes how the other presents, and generic approaches to either will be insufficient
The PDA profile requires substantially different support approaches; standard Autism practice focused on routine and compliance can cause active harm to PDA individuals
Physical health conditions directly affect energy budget, sensory profile, and mental health — holistic understanding of the whole person is not optional
Always ask: what else is happening here, and is it being seen and supported in its own right?
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar 2: Bringing It Together
posts.text:
Bringing It Together
Point 1 — Autistic Experience — is not a single concept. It is a layered, interconnected set of realities that shape every aspect of how an Autistic person moves through the world.
Spiky Profiles
Monotropism

Energy Accounting
Minority Stress
Violence & Exploitation
Co-occurrences
(Speaker notes: These seven dimensions do not operate independently. Monotropism shapes the energy cost of transitions. Minority stress compounds the energy deficit. Co-occurring conditions change the profile. Spiky profiles affect how all of these manifest and are perceived. Understanding Point One well means understanding how these threads weave together in any individual's life.)

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar: When Autistic people experience distress, the ecosystemic model asks us to look at the whole picture.
posts.text:
When Autistic people experience distress, the ecosystemic model asks us to look at the whole picture.
Not: 'What is wrong with this Autistic person?'
But: 'What is the mismatch between this Bodymind and this environment; and what structural factors are preventing those needs from being met?'
NeuroHub Community — Ecosystemic Model of Distress

Autistic Experience
The theoretical foundations for how Autistic people experience the world

Autistic People Are Not Failed Neurotypicals
Point 1 — Autistic Experience
Autistic people have a genuinely different neurological organisation
This produces genuinely different ways of processing, perceiving, and relating to the world
Much of what has been described as 'Autistic deficit' is Autistic difference encountering a world not designed for it
The question is not 'what went wrong?’ , it is 'what do different conditions look like?'
This distinction shapes the entire orientation of affirming practice
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar: Monotropism
posts.text:
Monotropism
Murray, Lesser & Lawson: a theory of Autistic cognitive style
Monotropic  (Autistic)
Intense focus directed at fewer interests or tasks at once
Deep cognitive and emotional resource poured into areas of focus
Extraordinary depth of engagement and pattern recognition
Disrupting or redirecting focus carries a real cost: not a choice or preference
Polytropic  (Neurotypical default)
Attention distributed broadly and flexibly across multiple streams
Easier shifting between competing demands
Context-switching feels lower-cost
The assumed default in most institutional and professional environments
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

The Double Empathy Problem
Dr Damian Milton: reconsidering where communication breakdown actually lies
When Autistic and non-Autistic people struggle to understand each other, that is a mutual phenomenon — not evidence of an Autistic deficit.
Non-Autistic people also struggle to understand Autistic people; this goes unexamined
Autistic people communicate and connect well with other Autistic people
The 'theory of mind deficit' framing positioned Autistic people as the problem, the double empathy problem distributes responsibility accurately
Communication difficulties in Autistic-neurotypical interactions are relational and context-dependent
For practitioners: if you find it hard to understand an Autistic person, the responsibility for bridging that gap is not theirs alone
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar: Experiencing the World Differently
posts.text:
Experiencing the World Differently
Point 1 — Autistic Experience
Different perceptual and cognitive architecture; not a broken version of neurotypicality
A different relationship to social scripting, implicit norms, and unspoken conventions
Strong pattern recognition; depth of knowledge and engagement in areas of focus
A tendency toward direct, literal communication; a strength in the right context
A different relationship to time, routine, predictability, and change
None of these are deficits. They are characteristics of a different kind of mind.
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

Sensory & Emotional Landscape
How Autistic people navigate the sensory environment and emotions

Sensory Processing Differences
Point 2 — Sensory & Emotional Landscape
Hypersensitivity and hyposensitivity are not fixed; many Autistic people experience both in the same modality
Sensory threshold shifts under cognitive and emotional load; what is manageable at baseline may be overwhelming under demand
Designing support from high-demand assessment contexts will miss a great deal
Interoception (internal body sense) is frequently atypical; hunger, pain, temperature, and emotional escalation can be harder to register
A person not noticing pain until it's severe is not being avoidant; their body-sense works differently
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar: Sensory Overload, Meltdown and Shutdown
posts.text:
Sensory Overload, Meltdown and Shutdown
Point 2 — Sensory & Emotional Landscape
Sensory overload: when input exceeds what the nervous system can process and regulate
Meltdown: intense, involuntary nervous system respon; distress, loss of language, emotional outburst
Shutdown: nervous system withdraws from input; a person may appear 'fine' precisely when they are most overwhelmed
Both are nervous system responses, not behavioural choices to be managed
Responding to them as behaviour problems compounds the distress
The appropriate response is reduction of demand and sensory load; not behaviour management
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

Alexithymia and Emotional Experience
Point 2 — Sensory & Emotional Landscape
Alexithymia: difficulty identifying and describing one's own emotional states; present in a significant proportion of Autistic people
This is not an absence of emotion; Autistic people often experience emotions with considerable intensity
What alexithymia affects is the ability to identify, name, and communicate about that emotion
Asking 'how are you feeling?' may not be a meaningful question in the way we assume
Emotional regulation becomes harder when sensory and cognitive load are already high, this is how the nervous system works under pressure, not a character failing
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar: Stimming
posts.text:
Stimming
Self-stimulatory behaviour serves important regulatory functions; it is not behaviour to be managed
What stimming does
Manages sensory input
Processes emotions
Maintains focus and attention
Regulates the nervous system
For practice
Suppressing stimming removes a regulatory tool
Adds significantly to the burden of masking
Environments that allow stimming are more supportive; not less professional
Examine your setting's implicit policies on movement and self-regulation
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

Autistic Burnout
A crisis of chronic disconnection, not occupational tiredness

What Is Autistic Burnout?
Dr Monique Botha: a specific experience distinct from occupational burnout
Pervasive Exhaustion
Not tiredness; a deep systemic depletion. Rest alone does not resolve it. The result of sustained demand beyond capacity in neurotypical environments.
Increased Sensitivity
Sensory and emotional thresholds lower. Previously manageable demands become overwhelming. The nervous system is depleted and under-resourced.
Skill Loss
Communication, executive function, self-care, and even language can become temporarily or persistently unavailable. This is real depletion, not regression.
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar: The Role of Masking
posts.text:
The Role of Masking
Point 3: Autistic Burnout
Masking: suppressing or modifying natural Autistic traits to appear neurotypical; scripting interactions, suppressing stimming, performing eye contact
Masking is exhausting; it consumes enormous cognitive and emotional resource
Because masking makes Autistic people appear to be coping, internal depletion is frequently invisible
Autistic people often describe late diagnosis as a relief; it explains a level of exhaustion they had been told was inexplicable
Chronic masking is strongly associated with burnout, depression, anxiety, and suicidality
Supporting Autistic people means creating conditions in which masking is not necessary; not rewarding or demanding it
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

Autistic burnout is not an internal event happening inside the Autistic person's Bodymind in isolation.
It is an ecosystemic signal; the Bodymind's response to sustained mismatch with the Immediate Environment, compounded by Power Structures that fail to provide accommodation or recognition.
NeuroHub Community — Ecosystemic Model of Distress

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar: Supporting Recovery From Burnout
posts.text:
Supporting Recovery From Burnout
Point 3 — Autistic Burnout
Genuine reduction in demand — not a brief break before returning to the same conditions
Space for the nervous system to regulate without performance pressure or expectation
Reduction of sensory load; restoration of routine and predictability
Removal of the expectation to mask or perform functioning
Advocate for adjustments that may go beyond institutional comfort zones
Name burnout clearly — not as regression, resistance, or deterioration
Pushing through burnout does not build resilience. It deepens the depletion.
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

Burnout Recovery Planning
NeuroHub Community has developed a web tool for developing a burnout recovery plan available from neurohubcommunity. org
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

Identity, Language & Disability Models
How autism is framed; and why framing is never neutral

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar: Two Models of Disability, A Single Paradigm
posts.text:
Two Models of Disability, A Single Paradigm
The models & Paradigms used to understand Autism determines what counts as a problem; and what counts as a solution
Medical Model
Locates the problem in the individual's neurology or behaviour. Goal: reduce, manage, or eliminate difference. Has produced compliance-based and normalisation interventions including ABA.
Social Model
Distinguishes impairment (neurological difference) from disability (what society creates for people with that difference). Changes the locus of intervention to environments and systems.
Neurodiversity Paradigm
Neurological variation is natural and valuable. Autistic people are not disordered. Challenges are produced by a world designed for a narrow band of neurological experience. Leans toward the social model of disability.
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar: Language and Identity
posts.text:
Language and Identity
Point 4: Identity, Language & Disability Models
Language is constitutive: it shapes how Autistic people understand themselves and how they are understood by others
NeuroHub uses identity-first language: 'Autistic person', 'Autistic people' — in line with community consensus (See our Autistic Language Preference Survey Report)
This reflects the position that Autism is not separate from a person but part of who they are
'Person with Autism' implies Autism is an add-on, separable from the Self; for most Autistic people, this does not reflect lived experience
Describing Autistic traits as deficits or symptoms sends a message about how Autistic people are valued
Individual preferences should always be honoured, but identity-first is the appropriate professional default
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

The Importance of Diagnosis
Point 4: Identity, Language & Disability Models
Women, girls, and people from racially minoritised communities have been historically missed; criteria were derived from a narrow demographic
Late diagnosis is common: many Autistic adults have spent decades being told their experiences are anxiety, personality disorder, or personal failure
Receiving a late diagnosis is often profoundly validating; it provides a framework for a lifetime of unrecognised experience
The absence of a formal diagnosis should not be used to withhold Autistic-affirming support
If someone presents as Autistic and experiences the world in Autistic ways, support them accordingly
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar: Trauma & Safety
posts.text:
Trauma & Safety
Autistic trauma, and what psychological safety requires in practice

Autistic People and Trauma
Point 5: Trauma & Safety
Autistic people experience trauma at significantly higher rates than the general population; not because Autism predisposes to it, but because of disproportionate exposure
High rates of bullying, social rejection, and abuse; including in institutional settings meant to provide support
Some interventions are themselves traumatic: forced eye contact, sensory dismissal, suppression of natural responses, cognitive behavioural therapies used inappropriately
Growing up undiagnosed is frequently experienced as traumatic; sustained confusion, difference without explanation, consistent messages that one's way of being is wrong
Trauma-informed practice is not optional for anyone working with Autistic people, it is a baseline requirement
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar: How Trauma Presents in Autistic People
posts.text:
How Trauma Presents in Autistic People
Point 5: Trauma & Safety
Trauma responses in Autistic people may not follow typical PTSD presentations; this is frequently misread in clinical contexts
Heightened sensory sensitivity may be simultaneously an Autistic trait and a trauma response
Difficulty with transitions, social withdrawal, emotional dysregulation may be Autistic characteristics, trauma responses, burnout, or all three simultaneously
This complexity is not a reason to avoid the question of trauma, it is a reason to approach it carefully
Take seriously what Autistic people themselves say about their experiences; do not over-attribute in either direction
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

Psychological Safety
Autistic people who do not feel safe cannot engage meaningfully with support
Predictability
Knowing what to expect and having that expectation honoured. Consistent structure and advance notice of changes.
Sensory Safety
An environment that does not overload the nervous system. Lighting, noise, and sensory demands considered and managed.
Relational Safety
A consistent, honest supporter who does not demand performance or masking to access help or to be believed.
Known Accurately
Autistic traits are not pathologised, misrepresented, or treated as problems to be corrected within the relationship.
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar: Re-traumatisation in Support Systems
posts.text:
Re-traumatisation in Support Systems
Support systems can (and do) re-traumatise Autistic people
Practitioners need to examine their own practice for where it inadvertently demands performance, dismisses Autistic experience, or requires self-justification to access support.
Diagnostic processes that are lengthy, intrusive, and conducted without affirming knowledge
Interventions that prioritise appearance and compliance over wellbeing
Being disbelieved, dismissed, or misdiagnosed over extended periods
Being required to perform functioning to access support; structural masking-on-demand
This examination is not comfortable. It is necessary.
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

Learning From The Autistic Community
Epistemic justice, community knowledge, and Nothing About Us Without Us

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar: Epistemic Justice
posts.text:
Epistemic Justice
Point 6: Learning From The Autistic Community
Epistemic injustice (Miranda Fricker): harm done when someone is wrongly judged as less credible as a knower because of their social identity
Autistic people have had their accounts of their own experiences dismissed, pathologised, or overridden by professional frameworks
The claim that Autistic people cannot accurately report their inner experience has been used to justify significant professional overreach, see Yergeau, 2018 and the concept of demi-rhetoricity in Autistic rhetorical framing.
Epistemic justice in autism practice means taking Autistic self-knowledge seriously; as the primary source, not one data point among many
Autistic people are the experts on their own lives. That is not a qualifier, it is the foundation.
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar: The Autistic Community as Knowledge Base
posts.text:
The Autistic Community as Knowledge Base
Point 6: Learning From The Autistic Community
Autistic-led organisations, scholars, writers, and advocates have produced an enormous body of knowledge about Autistic experience and wellbeing
Developed largely outside of (and often in direct response to) professional and clinical frameworks
This knowledge is not anecdotal. It is collective, evidenced, and accumulated over decades.
Much of what now constitutes best practice in affirming support was developed or shaped by Autistic thinkers over the past 30 years.
The neurodiversity paradigm itself emerged from Autistic community activism. The concept originated from thinkers on the INLV forum in the early 90’s.
Learning from the Autistic community is not a supplementary resource for practitioners, it is a core competency
NeuroHub Community Ltd  |  neurohubcommunity. org

Nothing About Us Without Us.
Services, frameworks, and practices that affect Autistic people should be designed with genuine Autistic involvement; not token consultation, but real co-production and Autistic leadership.
Who are you learning from?
Disability Rights Principle — applied to Autistic practice

Bringing It Together
The framework is not a checklist.
It is a lens; a set of questions to bring to every professional encounter with an Autistic person, and to every environment, system, or service that is meant to support them.
Ecosystemic model  ·  Six points  ·  One orienting question: what does this Autistic person need to flourish as themselves?

posts.title: Supporting Autistic People Webinar: Supporting Autistic people well means creating the conditions for Autistic people to flourish as Autistic people; not as app
posts.text:
Supporting Autistic people well means creating the conditions for Autistic people to flourish as Autistic people; not as approximations of neurotypicality.
Reduce the demand to mask, make environments safer. speak honestly. Believe what Autistic people tell you about their own lives, and hold the systemic picture.
NeuroHub Community Ltd — Six-Point Framework

NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
