Institutional Discrimination
When the systems designed to help become part of the harm

posts.title: Surviving The System - Autism Addiction: The Catch-22: No Help Until You Fix the Other Thing
posts.text:
The Catch-22: No Help Until You Fix the Other Thing
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
Two services. Two referrals. Two rejections. Zero help.
MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES
“We cannot support you while you are actively using substances. Please engage with substance use services first.”
↔
SUBSTANCE USE SERVICES
“We cannot support you until your mental health is stable. Please engage with mental health services first.”
(Speaker notes: Both services were technically following their referral criteria. Both were technically correct. There was no third option. There was no pathway. There was just — nothing. This is structural. It is not individual worker failure. It is a design failure. And it is happening to Autistic people every day.)

NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
“You can’t be Autistic, you make eye contact.”
“You seem to understand social situations too well.”
“You’re using autism as an excuse for your behaviour.”
“Your difficulties are caused by your substance use, not autism.”
This is epistemic injustice: the denial of someone’s credibility as a knower of their own experience.
(Speaker notes: Miranda Fricker's concept of epistemic injustice is useful here. This denial had material consequences.)

PART 3
The BPD Misdiagnosis
How a diagnostic label became a weapon

posts.title: Surviving The System - Autism Addiction: Labelled, Filed, and Left: Years Under the Wrong Diagnosis
posts.text:
Labelled, Filed, and Left: Years Under the Wrong Diagnosis
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
The diagnosis was wrong — but its consequences were very real.
The BPD Label in Practice
Every crisis was read as 'manipulative behaviour'. Every emotional response was evidence of 'instability'.
The Double Stigma
BPD carries profound stigma within clinical services.
What Was Actually Happening
The Masking Trap
(Speaker notes: The BPD diagnosis was not made maliciously. Research suggests significant diagnostic overlap between BPD presentations and unidentified Autistic experience — particularly in women and people assigned female at birth. The emotional intensity, the relationship difficulties, the identity disturbance — these can all arise from Autistic experience in hostile environments.)

Compounded Stigma: When Labels Become Barriers to Care
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
Stigma does not exist in isolation: it compounds.
Addiction
Stigma
+
BPD
Stigma

Psychosis

Autistic
Invisibility
= A person that many services decided was too complex, too difficult, too non-compliant to help
Referrals were delayed or refused without clear justification
(Speaker notes: It felt like being made illegitimate. The person behind the labels disappeared.)

PART 4
The Twelve-Step Dead End
(Speaker notes: They work for many people.)

posts.title: Surviving The System - Autism Addiction: The Twelve Steps: A Framework Not Built for Autistic Minds
posts.text:
The Twelve Steps: A Framework Not Built for Autistic Minds
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
Implicit Social Scripts
Meetings rely on unwritten social rules; when to speak, how to respond, what is appropriate. These were opaque and distressing to navigate.
Spiritual Framework
The 12-step model is built around surrender to a Higher Power.
Performance of Recovery
There was an expectation to perform a particular kind of recovering person; emotionally expressive, sociable, grateful.
Sensory Environment
Cramped rooms, coffee smells, people talking over each other, unpredictable emotional intensity. Meetings were regularly overwhelming to the point of shutdown.
The Sponsor Relationship
Moral Inventory as Shame
Step Four asks for fearless moral inventory.
(Speaker notes: Each of these is not a personal failing. Each of these is a feature of Autistic neurology meeting a programme designed without Autistic people in mind. The problem is not us. The problem is the assumption that twelve steps is a universal pathway, when evidence suggests it is culturally and neurologically specific. Because it is the default. Because it is cheap. Because we have not invested in alternatives.)

posts.title: Surviving The System - Autism Addiction: When Recovery Programmes Make Things Worse
posts.text:
When Recovery Programmes Make Things Worse
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
This is not unusual. Research on Autistic people and substance use recovery consistently finds that approaches requiring social conformity, unwritten rules, and spiritual surrender are poorly matched to Autistic cognition and sensory experience.
While Attending
Increased anxiety before every meeting
Shutdown following most meetings
Shame spirals from 'moral inventory'
Sense of total failure at recovery
After Stopping
Reduction in anxiety
More capacity for genuine self-reflection
Ability to build real connections
Recovery became possible
(Speaker notes: The change was stark. If a person's mental health consistently deteriorates in a recovery programme, and improves when they leave it — what does that tell us about the programme?)

PART 5
Community as Recovery
How connecting with other Autistic people changed everything
(Speaker notes: This is the turn in the story. After years of failed professional interventions, the thing that made recovery possible was not a programme. It was people. Autistic people. People who understood.)

NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
Recovery did not happen in a clinic or a meeting hall. It happened in community with other Autistic people.
BEFORE
AFTER
→
→
Social rules were opaque and exhausting
→
We built our own relational norms together
→
(Speaker notes: When you no longer have to be someone else in order to be safe, the need for the substances that made it possible to perform that starts to reduce.)

posts.title: Surviving The System - Autism Addiction: What Autistic Community Provided That Services Could Not
posts.text:
What Autistic Community Provided That Services Could Not
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
Authentic Identity
Shared Language
Non-Judgmental Witness
Community provided a kind of witnessing that clinical spaces had never offered.
Practical Solidarity
People who had navigated similar systems shared knowledge, strategies, and support.
Reduced Masking Load
Hope Through Visibility
Not cured; but thriving on their own terms. That was profoundly powerful.
(Speaker notes: Every one of these things — community provided them without training, without a clinical model, without a protocol. Not because community is magic, but because belonging is a fundamental human need. And for Autistic people, finding a community where we do not have to mask to belong is not a nice-to-have. It is therapeutic. It is, for many of us, the foundation on which everything else becomes possible.)

posts.title: Surviving The System - Autism Addiction: Building Community Intentionally: Autistic Inclusive Meets
posts.text:
Building Community Intentionally: Autistic Inclusive Meets
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
Recovery is not an individual achievement. It is a collective condition.
Autistic-Led
Created and run by Autistic people; not services for us, built without us
Sensory Awareness
Environments designed with our sensory needs in mind from the start
Communication Plurality
Multiple ways to communicate are welcomed; not just verbal, neurotypical interaction
Non-Pathologising
Autistic experience is not treated as deficit; it is understood and valued
(Speaker notes: These spaces are not therapeutic programmes. They are not recovery services. They are Autistic community — and in being Autistic community, they do something therapeutic that no recovery service has managed to do for many of us. That's worth naming. It's worth asking why. And it's worth asking what we could learn from it.)

PART 6
What We Need From Systems
Moving from harm to genuine support for Autistic people in recovery

posts.title: Surviving The System - Autism Addiction: What Systems Must Change: A Non-Negotiable List
posts.text:
What Systems Must Change: A Non-Negotiable List
NeuroHub Community Ltd. |  neurohubcommunity. org
End the mental health / substance use split
Co-occurring needs must be supported together. The referral loop must end.
Autistic-specific pathways
Substance use recovery for Autistic people cannot be neurotypical recovery with minor adjustments.
Train for masking and late diagnosis
Clinicians must understand that Autistic people may not 'present' as Autistic under assessment conditions.
Take misdiagnosis seriously
BPD diagnoses in people without formal Autistic assessment should be reviewed. The pipeline between BPD and Autistic identification must be shortened.
Believe Autistic people about our own experience
Epistemic justice is not optional. Our testimony about our own lives must be treated as credible and valuable.
Fund Autistic-led community
Autistic community is not supplementary to recovery; for many of us, it is the foundation. Fund it accordingly.
(Speaker notes: These are not suggestions. These are the minimum requirements for services to stop actively harming Autistic people who are trying to access help. System change is not optional. It is a matter of life and death.)

posts.title: Surviving The System - Autism Addiction: CONCLUSION
posts.text:
CONCLUSION
Recovery is possible.
But it requires the right conditions.
Addiction in Autistic people is a response to an ecosystem that was not designed for us
Systems must stop gatekeeping and start providing genuinely co-occurring support
The twelve-step model is not a universal solution; and for many Autistic people, it causes harm
Community connection with other Autistic people is not supplementary, it can be the foundation of recovery
Nothing about us, without us; this applies to recovery as much as to anywhere else

posts.title: Talking To Professionals
posts.text:
Talking To Professionals

Objectives
Acknowledgement
Navigating professionals can feel like a full-time job, especially when you’re exhausted and trying to advocate for someone you love.
Objectives
Understand why communication with professionals often breaks down.
Learn tools to make conversations more effective.
Feel more confident and in control during meetings.

Why Communication Can Be So Hard

Systemic Challenges
Power imbalance: Professionals hold decision-making power and specialist knowledge.
Different priorities: Parents focus on lived reality and emotional impact; professionals focus on process, risk, or outcomes.
Jargon and language barriers: How professional language can feel alienating or pathologising.
Cognitive load and stress: When you’re in fight-or-flight, communication gets harder.
Neurodivergence and trauma: Many families are autistic, ADHD, or trauma-exposed themselves; communication needs may differ.

posts.title: Talking To Professionals: From “Us vs Them” To Collaboration
posts.text:
From “Us vs Them” To Collaboration
See yourself as an expert-by-experience. You bring lived expertise; professionals bring technical expertise. Both are needed.
Use “we” language. instead of “You’re not listening.”
Acknowledge shared goals. “We both want them to thrive.”
Ask clarifying questions. Instead of accepting unclear information, e. g. “Can you explain what that means in plain English?”
Think about the outcome. What do we want? Is it available/possible? Are we asking the right people?
Clarify people’s roles. Is this the right professional for the matter at hand?
Manage your own energy. Choose your battles, don’t waste energy on fights that do not help
Are we following the right process to get the outcome that we want?

Practical Tools & Strategies (Before The Meeting)
Ground yourself in the present
You can use sensory experiences and grounding techniques to anchor yourself to a feeling of safety.
Build your confidence
Dress and posture yourself as confident
Take time to reflect on your own wellbeing
Nest yourself in a safe activity or environment to lower your emotional arousal

Practical Tools & Strategies (Before The Meeting)
Write down key points you need to get across. Then edit and prioritise.
Bring short notes or examples (logs, letters, anything that provides evidence).
If overwhelmed, ask someone to attend with you or take notes.
Ensure notes are taken, you are able to record meetings for personal use only.
Make sure any minutes are agreed and circulated.

posts.title: Talking To Professionals: Practical Tools & Strategies (During The Meeting)
posts.text:
Practical Tools & Strategies (During The Meeting)
Use calm, factual language.
Repeat back what you’ve heard to check understanding (“So what you’re saying is…”).
Ask for timescales, actions, and responsibilities (“Who will do this, and by when?”)
If overwhelmed, do not agree to anything, set a time to come back.
Ensure you  have contact details for everyone who has actions.

Practical Tools & Strategies (After The Meeting)
Summarise in an email (“Just to confirm what we agreed today…”).
Keep a record of all correspondence.
Follow up politely but firmly on missed actions.
Allow yourself processing time to reflect and think about the outcome.
“was this useful?”

posts.title: Understanding Autistic Wellbeing
posts.text:
Understanding Autistic Wellbeing

How common are mental health
Problems in Autistic populations?
Research has suggested that at least 50% of Autistic people have a mental health problem, going up to 72. 4% when the person is Autistic and ADHD (Pehlivanidis et al, 2020).
This is a factor in why the Autistic suicide rate is 9x higher than the general population across all age groups, with Autistic children being 28x more likely to think about or attempt suicide. Autistic people represent 11% of all suicides (RCPsych, n. d.)
In the 86 days leading up to the first lock down, and the 56 after, Autistic children and young people represent 25% of suicides (RCPsych, n. d.)
It is clear from these statistics that mental health problems are a significant area of need for Autistic people, and vital that we understand the mechanics of how and why they occur.

Theories of Autistic Experience
We will look at-
Monotropism
Masking
Energy Accounting
The Double Empathy Problem
Sensory Differences and Sensory Trauma
The Autistic Environment (The Golden Equation)
Victimisation of Autistic Individuals
The Six Stages of Autistic Discovery
We will consider how each applies to Autistic Experience

Monotropism
The theory that Autistic people’s brains tend towards hyperfocused attention tunnels, and have limited attentional resources to allocate to tasks (Murray et al, 2005).
As opposed to neurotypical people who are able to split their attentional resources across multiple competing demands simultaneously.

Monotropism Continued…
Monotropic Split
Monotropic Spiral
Meerkat Mode

posts.title: Understanding Autistic Wellbeing: Autistic Burnout
posts.text:
Autistic Burnout
Autistic burnout occurs when the expectations and demands on an Autistic person exceed their cognitive capacity
Features of Autistic burnout include loss of skills, chronic exhaustion, and sensory & emotional dysregulation (Raymaker et al, 2020)
Atypical Burnout- Burnout doesn’t alway look like the typical idea of not being able to do anything
Autistic burnout is a risk factor for mental health issues and suicidality (Raymaker et al, 2020).

Monotropism and Autistic Mental Health
Autistic people need to be allowed to hyperfocus
When we are forced to split our attention, a community created concept called monotropic split (Adkin, 2022), it has a detrimental effect on our wellbeing
Attention isn’t always conscious, for example, a parent always has it in the back of their mind that they are a parent and need to care for their child
In this sense, we can think of mental health issues occurring from the cognitive trauma of conforming to a non-Autistic way of cognition and engagement with the world.

Masking
This is also known as ‘camouflaging’.
It refers to the act of concealing one’s Autistic traits to appear more neurotypical.
Commonly misunderstood, it is not necessarily a conscious choice, it is a survival reflex, we cannot simply choose to unmask.
Masking takes a tremendous toll on cognitive resources and energy.
Many Autistic adults are missed because they have become so adept at masking (Pearson & Rose, 2021).

posts.title: Understanding Autistic Wellbeing: Masking and Autistic Wellbeing
posts.text:
Masking and Autistic Wellbeing
Masking is a survival reflex that we use to stay safe in a society that mistreats us
It can be imagine as a source of monotropic split
Constantly needing to manage how one comes across to others is an extra demand that we need to pay attention to on top of other demands
It affects our sense of Self and identity, and can lead to mental health problems and suicidality (Pearson & Rose, 2021)

Energy Accounting
Energy accounting is the concept that Autistic people have to manage their psychological and physical energy levels (or cognitive resources) throughout the day.
Colloquially known as ‘Spoon Theory’.
When an Autistic person regularly exceeds their energy budget, this can lead to Burnout, which may result in a lessened ability to function daily and an increased observability of Autistic traits.

Energy Accounting and Autistic
Wellbeing
It is vital that Autistic people are allowed to maintain boundaries with regard to how much cognitive labour they perform
If an Autistic person does not “have the spoons” to do something, they should not be forced
Forcing an Autistic person to out-perform their cognitive resources does not build resilience, it leads to Autistic burnout
It can take months or years to recover from burnout

posts.title: Understanding Autistic Wellbeing: The Double Empathy Problem
posts.text:
The Double Empathy Problem
Posits that Autistic empathy, emotional, and communicative reciprocity is not in deficit, but instead different to that of non-Autistic people.
This means that Autistic-Autistic communication works better than Autistic-Neurotypical communication.
Autistic people are labelled as disordered in this area because of neuronormativity and marginalisation (Milton et al, 2023).

The Double Empathy Problem
in Practice
When Autistic people are told that they lack communication skills and empathy they can internalise that ableism
This kind of validation can impact on the Autistic person’s self-esteem presenting a risk to their mental health
It is important for Autistic people to have the opportunity to socialise with other Autistic people in a natural way
You wouldn’t expect a fish to learn how to live out of water, so why would you expect an Autistic to empathise or communicate in a non-Autistic way?

Sensory Differences and Sensory
Trauma
Autistic people have individual sensory profiles.
What may be exciting and restorative for one, may trigger trauma responses in another.
Our experience of sensory stimuli is different to that of non-Autistic people
Sensory Trauma occurs when a sensory experience is overwhelming or painful, and inescapable for the Autistic person (Fulton et al, 2020)

posts.title: Understanding Autistic Wellbeing: Sensory Trauma and Autistic Wellbeing
posts.text:
Sensory Trauma and Autistic Wellbeing
Sensory trauma is unavoidable in our current society (Fulton et al, 2020)
Sensory trauma can rapidly deplete cognitive resources or ‘spoons’
Excessive exposure to overwhelming sensory environments can result in increased frequency of meltdowns, physical illness, and complex mental health issues. Autistic people also anecdotally report drug and alcohol use to cope with sensory trauma.
It is vital that Autistic people have access to sensory safe spaces that are tailored to their individual preferences and needs

The Autistic Environment
(The Golden Equation)
Autism + Environment = Outcome

The Autistic Environment
(The Golden Equation)
The Autistic person’s individual profile plus the environment that they are in will directly create the outcomes achieved by and for the Autistic person.
If the environment that an Autistic person exists in is not well suited to their needs, they will experience negative outcomes and decreased wellbeing
It is important to take a person-centred, strengths-based approach to creating and curating the Autistic person's environment
The Autistic person should be allowed the autonomy to curate their own environment where possible
Autistic people anecdotally report environmental factors as being one of the most significant in the development of mental health problems

posts.title: Understanding Autistic Wellbeing: Victimisation of Autistic Individuals
posts.text:
Victimisation of Autistic Individuals
Autistic people are victimised at a higher rate than the general population
We experience mate crime, criminal exploitation, harassment, and structural oppression far more commonly than neurotypical people (Pearson et al, 2023)
Autistic people also occupy other intersections of race, gender and sexual identity, further disability, and class inequality. Any of these may compound the experience
This has a direct impact on our mental health
We must ensure that Autistic people are safeguarded without removing autonomy

Autism and Substance Use
Autistic people are more likely to report self-medicating with drugs and alcohol (Weir et al, 2021)
The same research also found that chronic pain, eating disorders, anxiety, and depression were significant factors for Autistic substance users
Further research we did that is also in review found that Autistic people report that substance misuse treatment services are failing to appropriately support Autistic service users.

The Six Stages of Autistic Discovery
Autistic mental health can and will change over time
It is important to meet the person where they are
Aucademy CIC has put together the following infographic on “The Six Stages of Autistic Discovery”

The Six Stages of Autistic Discovery
Denial
Depression
Acceptance
Embracing
Bargaining
Anger
They do not necessarily occur in a particular order, these are just six common reactions to discovering ones own Autistic Identity
It stands to reason that an Autistic persons mental health may change over the course of understanding themselves

posts.title: Understanding Autistic Wellbeing: Summary
posts.text:
Summary
There are multiple factors at play with Autistic mental health
An Autistic person in an environment suited to them is more likely to see good mental health outcomes
A balance is needed between safeguarding and autonomy
Thought must be given to where an Autistic person is in their journey of self-discovery
Services supporting Autistic people need to be neurodiversity affirming and culturally competent in Autistic experience

posts.title: Understanding Neurodivergent Experience: What is monotropism?
posts.text:
What is monotropism?
Conceptualised by Murray, Lesser & Lawson
Originally thought to be the underlying cognition for autism, it is slowly being applied to other diagnoses such as ADHD and schizophrenia
Essentially describes the attention style of Autistic and some other neurodivergent people.

What is monotropism?
•Autistic Inertia
•Sensory Differences
•Social Differences
•Focused Interests

How does monotropism impact the neurodivergent professional?
Professionals may find themselves hypefocused on a particular task, and shut everything else out. This can result in ignoring self-care needs or other external demands on attention
Inertia may mean that a longer and more structured transition period is needed between tasks
Monotropic split may occur when competing demands repeatedly encroach on a person’s current focus.

What is monotropic split?
It describes a specific kind of cognitive trauma caused by competing demands on a monotropic brain.
The monotropic person is unable to regulate the amount of attention they apply to multiple demands and effectively overtax their cognitive resources.

posts.title: Understanding Neurodivergent Experience: What is masking?
posts.text:
What is masking?
Autistic masking (also referred to in the literature as camouflaging, compensation, and most recently “adaptive morphing”) is the conscious or unconscious suppression of natural responses and adoption of alternatives across a range of domains including social interaction, sensory experience, cognition, movement, and behaviour.
(Pearson & Rose, 2021)
Masking can be seen as a form of identity management
Research indicates that this can be both conscious and unconscious.
Masking is incredibly taxing on cognitive resources and can lead to monotropic split or burnout

Risks associated with masking
As well as monotropic split masking has been linked to;
Worsening mental health
Suicidality

What is the double empathy problem?
Explains differences in presentations of empathy between Autistic and non-Autistic people (Milton, 2012)
Explains them through differences in cultural experience
Used to reposition Autistic communication as difference rather than in deficit.
Suggests that two different cultural groups can never fully empathise with each other as they will never have the same experiences of society.

posts.title: Understanding Neurodivergent Experience: The double empathy problem in practice
posts.text:
The double empathy problem in practice
This has the potential to lead to misunderstandings and disagreements in the workplace.
Autistic people are often accused of being rude or uncaring because the recipient of communication does not understand Autistic communication.
It’s important to note that the expectation should be for each person to occupy the middle ground.
The onus should not be on the Autistic person to communicate in a neurotypical way or meet neuronormative standards.

What is Autistic burnout?
When an Autistic person regularly exceeds their energy budget, this can lead to Burnout, which may result in a lessened ability to function daily and an increased observability of Autistic traits (Raymaker et al, 2020).
Linked to decreased wellbeing and suicidality among Autistic people

How is burnout conceptualised?
Cognitive overload (monotropic split)
Severe mental and physical exhaustion
Interpersonal withdrawal
Significant reduction in multiple areas of functioning
Confusion and/or Difficulty with executive functioning and/or Dissociative states
Increased intensity of Autistic traits and/or reduced capacity to mask
This not being better described by other psychiatric condition.
(Arnold et al, 2023; Higgins et al, 2021)

Problems with observational models
“Female  autism”
Misconceptions around masking (only girls can mask, etc.)
Challenging behaviour
Observational models are medical model focused and locate the problem within the person

posts.title: Understanding Neurodivergent Experience: Problems with observational models
posts.text:

The progress we have made in understanding Autistic experience has come from Autistic people rather than observational approaches-
-Double empathy
-Masking
-Stimming
-Interoception
-Exposure anxiety
“In common with the occupational burnout construct, further work is needed to disambiguate autistic burnout from depression and other conditions that are potential misdiagnoses.” (Arnold et al, 2023)

Problems with Observational Models
“There are infinite possible interactions between [a monotropic] person and their environment. Adkin (2023)

Atypical Burnout
Not actually all that rare, named as such because it refers to burnout outside of the “typical” observational models.
People who can’t stop still burnout.
“The use of the word atypical is not to create a neat category for an observable form of burnout. What we are referring to is burnout that might look different to the typical “depressive” understanding. In our experience it is not at all rare or atypical. We come across this time and again.”

ADHD and Autistic burnout
Anecdotal evidence that AuDHD people are more likely to experience atypical forms of burnout
May make it harder to recover from burnout due to need for constant stimulation

Atypical Burnout
People in atypical burnout may appear manic, delusional, paranoid, or any number of other distressed states.
While it should be taken on a case by case basis, it’s reasonable to ensure the person sees a psychiatrist to rule out any contributing mental health factors.

Victimisation and bullying
The Equalities Act 2010 was put in place to help protect employees against harassment for reasons such as being disabled or having an impairment. Some examples of possible harassment are:
Verbal abuse
Asking very personal questions – for example about a disability
Making rude gestures or facial expressions

posts.title: Understanding Neurodivergent Experience: Victimisation and bullying
posts.text:
Victimisation and bullying
While there are no solid statistics on workplace bullying in the UK, it is a big enough issue for major national charities such as NAS to have pages dedicated to it.
Much bullying of neurodivergent people can be traced back to neuronormativity and ableism.
“Our findings showed that a lot of autistic people think it is normal to be hurt by people you know because it has happened to them so much. This makes many autistic people feel like they need to mask parts of themselves to stay safe, but this also makes them really exhausted. It took some people a long time to realise what had happened to them was wrong, and it was hard to ask for help. People who did ask for help often had bad experiences with professionals (e. g. police) who did not know much about autistic people.” (Pearson et al, 2022)

Suicidality and Early mortality among Autistic people
Autistic adults are 9x more likely to die by suicide than general population (Royal College of Psychiatrists)
This has been linked to trauma, masking, and Autistic burnout
Average lifespan of Autistic people noticeably shorter, it is around 6 years less than the general population (O’Nions et al, 2024)
Alongside suicide is the risk of co-occuring health conditions that may go unaddressed due to healthcare inequality.

Autistic behaviour and communication
Stimming
Infodumping
Direct/blunt communication

posts.title: Understanding Neurodivergent Experience: What is stimming?
posts.text:
What is stimming?
Stimming is short for Self-stimulatory behaviour
Refers to repetitive actions performed by an Autistic person.
Ranges from hand flapping, through to vocal noises.
You can stim using any sense.
It is often a form of self-regulation. Both for senses and emotions.

What is infodumping?
Infodumping refers to the communication of information by a neurodivegent person (usually Autistic).
The person will “dump” a huge quantity of information on a topic in high volume and detail.
One of the forms of Autistic communication that is often discriminated against by neurotypical people.

Why do Autistic people tend to have blunt or direct communication
Autistic people need highly detailed communication.
Without this information we often find it difficult to communicate.
This means that often we are seen is blunt or rude, when what we need is direct and detailed communication.
Ongoing research by Rachel Cullen is exploring an “Autistic language hypothesis” that suggests Autistic people use and process language differently.

How to support a neurodivergent person
Don’t invalidate
Believe them about their experience
Avoid unnecessary demands
Allow for sensory breaks
Curate sensory environment
Do not create the expectation of acting “normal”
Do not judge the person based on what you think is or isn’t appropriate unless harm is clearly being done
Be a safe and trustworthy person

What is autism?
To meet diagnostic criteria for ASD according to DSM-5, a child must have persistent deficits in each of three areas of social communication and interaction (see A. 1. through A. 3. below) plus at least two of four types of restricted, repetitive behaviors (see B. 1. through B. 4. below).
Persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts, as manifested by the following, currently or by history (examples are illustrative, not exhaustive; see text):
Deficits in social-emotional reciprocity, ranging, for example, from abnormal social approach and failure of normal back-and-forth conversation; to reduced sharing of interests, emotions, or affect; to failure to initiate or respond to social interactions.
Deficits in nonverbal communicative behaviors used for social interaction, ranging, for example, from poorly integrated verbal and nonverbal communication; to abnormalities in eye contact and body language or deficits in understanding and use of gestures; to a total lack of facial expressions and nonverbal communication.
Deficits in developing, maintaining, and understanding relationships, ranging, for example, from difficulties adjusting behavior to suit various social contexts; to difficulties in sharing imaginative play or in making friends; to absence of interest in peers.

Stereotyped or repetitive motor movements, use of objects, or speech (e. g. , simple motor stereotypes, lining up toys or flipping objects, echolalia, idiosyncratic phrases).
Insistence on sameness, inflexible adherence to routines, or ritualized patterns of verbal or nonverbal behavior (e. g. , extreme distress at small changes, difficulties with transitions, rigid thinking patterns, greeting rituals, need to take same route or eat same food every day).
Highly restricted, fixated interests that are abnormal in intensity or focus (e. g. , strong attachment to or preoccupation with unusual objects, excessively circumscribed or perseverative interests).
Hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment (e. g. apparent indifference to pain/temperature, adverse response to specific sounds or textures, excessive smelling or touching of objects, visual fascination with lights or movement).

posts.text:
What is ADHD?
People with ADHD show a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity–impulsivity that interferes with functioning or development:
Inattention: Six or more symptoms of inattention for children up to age 16 years, or five or more for adolescents age 17 years and older and adults; symptoms of inattention have been present for at least 6 months, and they are inappropriate for developmental level:
Often fails to give close attention to details or makes careless mistakes in schoolwork, at work, or with other activities.
Often has trouble holding attention on tasks or play activities.
Often does not seem to listen when spoken to directly.
Often does not follow through on instructions and fails to finish schoolwork, chores, or duties in the workplace (e. g. , loses focus, side-tracked).
Often has trouble organizing tasks and activities.
Often avoids, dislikes, or is reluctant to do tasks that require mental effort over a long period of time (such as schoolwork or homework).
Often loses things necessary for tasks and activities (e. g. school materials, pencils, books, tools, wallets, keys, paperwork, eyeglasses, mobile telephones).
Is often easily distracted
Is often forgetful in daily activities.

posts.text:
What is ADHD?
2. Hyperactivity and Impulsivity: Six or more symptoms of hyperactivity-impulsivity for children up to age 16 years, or five or more for adolescents age 17 years and older and adults; symptoms of hyperactivity-impulsivity have been present for at least 6 months to an extent that is disruptive and inappropriate for the person’s developmental level:
Often fidgets with or taps hands or feet, or squirms in seat.
Often leaves seat in situations when remaining seated is expected.
Often runs about or climbs in situations where it is not appropriate (adolescents or adults may be limited to feeling restless).
Often unable to play or take part in leisure activities quietly.
Is often “on the go” acting as if “driven by a motor”.
Often talks excessively.
Often blurts out an answer before a question has been completed.
Often has trouble waiting their turn.
Often interrupts or intrudes on others (e. g. , butts into conversations or games)

What will we be covering?
Monotropism
Masking
The Double Empathy Problem
Burnout
Victimisation and bullying
Pathological Demand Avoidance

What is monotropism?
Conceptualised by Murray, Lesser & Lawson
Originally thought to be the underlying cognition for autism, it is slowly being applied to other diagnoses such as ADHD and schizophrenia
Essentially describes the attention style of Autistic and some other neurodivergent people.

What is monotropism?
•Autistic Inertia
•Sensory Differences
•Social Differences
•Focused Interests

How does monotropism impact the neurodivergent professional?
Professionals may find themselves hypefocused on a particular task, and shut everything else out. This can result in ignoring self-care needs or other external demands on attention
Inertia may mean that a longer and more structured transition period is needed between tasks
Monotropic split may occur when competing demands repeatedly encroach on a person’s current focus.

What is monotropic split?
It describes a specific kind of cognitive trauma caused by competing demands on a monotropic brain.
The monotropic person is unable to regulate the amount of attention they apply to multiple demands and effectively overtax their cognitive resources.

posts.title: Working with Neurodivergent staff: What is masking?
posts.text:
What is masking?
Autistic masking (also referred to in the literature as camouflaging, compensation, and most recently “adaptive morphing”) is the conscious or unconscious suppression of natural responses and adoption of alternatives across a range of domains including social interaction, sensory experience, cognition, movement, and behaviour.
(Pearson & Rose, 2021)
Masking can be seen as a form of identity management
Research indicates that this can be both conscious and unconscious.
Masking is incredibly taxing on cognitive resources and can lead to monotropic split or burnout

Risks associated with masking
As well as monotropic split masking has been linked to;
Worsening mental health
Suicidality

What is the double empathy problem?
Explains differences in presentations of empathy between Autistic and non-Autistic people (Milton, 2012)
Explains them through differences in cultural experience
Used to reposition Autistic communication as difference rather than in deficit.
Suggests that two different cultural groups can never fully empathise with each other as they will never have the same experiences of society.

posts.title: Working with Neurodivergent staff: The double empathy problem in practice
posts.text:
The double empathy problem in practice
This has the potential to lead to misunderstandings and disagreements in the workplace.
Autistic people are often accused of being rude or uncaring because the recipient of communication does not understand Autistic communication.
It’s important to note that the expectation should be for each person to occupy the middle ground.
The onus should not be on the Autistic person to communicate in a neurotypical way or meet neuronormative standards.

What is Autistic burnout?
When an Autistic person regularly exceeds their energy budget, this can lead to Burnout, which may result in a lessened ability to function daily and an increased observability of Autistic traits (Raymaker et al, 2020).
Linked to decreased wellbeing and suicidality among Autistic people

How is burnout conceptualised by observational models?
Cognitive overload (monotropic split)
Severe mental and physical exhaustion
Interpersonal withdrawal
Significant reduction in multiple areas of functioning
Confusion and/or Difficulty with executive functioning and/or Dissociative states
Increased intensity of Autistic traits and/or reduced capacity to mask
This not being better described by other psychiatric condition.
(Arnold et al, 2023; Higgins et al, 2021)

Problems with observational models
“Female  autism”
Misconceptions around masking (only girls can mask, etc.)
Challenging behaviour
Observational models are medical model focused and locate the problem within the person

posts.title: Working with Neurodivergent staff: Problems with observational models
posts.text:
Problems with observational models
The progress we have made in understanding Autistic experience has come from Autistic people rather than observational approaches-
-Double empathy
-Masking
-Stimming
-Interoception
-Exposure anxiety
“In common with the occupational burnout construct, further work is needed to disambiguate autistic burnout from depression and other conditions that are potential misdiagnoses.” (Arnold et al, 2023)

Problems with Observational Models
“There are infinite possible interactions between [a monotropic] person and their environment. Adkin (2023)

Atypical Burnout
Not actually all that rare, named as such because it refers to burnout outside of the “typical” observational models.
People who can’t stop still burnout.
“The use of the word atypical is not to create a neat category for an observable form of burnout. What we are referring to is burnout that might look different to the typical “depressive” understanding. In our experience it is not at all rare or atypical. We come across this time and again.”

ADHD and Autistic burnout
Anecdotal evidence that AuDHD people are more likely to experience atypical forms of burnout
May make it harder to recover from burnout due to need for constant stimulation

Atypical Burnout
People in atypical burnout may appear manic, delusional, paranoid, or any number of other distressed states.
While it should be taken on a case by case basis, it’s reasonable to ensure the person sees a psychiatrist to rule out any contributing mental health factors.

Victimisation and bullying
The Equalities Act 2010 was put in place to help protect employees against harassment for reasons such as being disabled or having an impairment. Some examples of possible harassment are:
Verbal abuse
Asking very personal questions – for example about a disability
Making rude gestures or facial expressions
Making offensive comments
Mention (Pearson & Rose, 2022)

posts.title: Working with Neurodivergent staff: Victimisation and bullying
posts.text:
Victimisation and bullying
While there are no solid statistics on workplace bullying in the UK, it is a big enough issue for major national charities such as NAS to have pages dedicated to it.
Much bullying of neurodivergent people can be traced back to neuronormativity and ableism.
“Our findings showed that a lot of autistic people think it is normal to be hurt by people you know because it has happened to them so much. This makes many autistic people feel like they need to mask parts of themselves to stay safe, but this also makes them really exhausted. It took some people a long time to realise what had happened to them was wrong, and it was hard to ask for help. People who did ask for help often had bad experiences with professionals (e. g. police) who did not know much about autistic people.” (Pearson et al, 2022)

Suicidality and Early mortality among Autistic people
Autistic adults are 9x more likely to die by suicide than general population (Royal College of Psychiatrists)
This has been linked to trauma, masking, and Autistic burnout
Average lifespan of Autistic people noticeably shorter, it is around 6 years less than the general population (O’Nions et al, 2024)
Alongside suicide is the risk of co-occuring health conditions that may go unaddressed due to healthcare inequality.

Autistic behaviour and communication
Stimming
Infodumping
Direct/blunt communication

posts.title: Working with Neurodivergent staff: What is stimming?
posts.text:
What is stimming?
Stimming is short for Self-stimulatory behaviour
Refers to repetitive actions performed by an Autistic person.
Ranges from hand flapping, through to vocal noises.
You can stim using any sense.
It is often a form of self-regulation. Both for senses and emotions.

What is infodumping?
Infodumping refers to the communication of information by a neurodivegent person (usually Autistic).
The person will “dump” a huge quantity of information on a topic in high volume and detail.
One of the forms of Autistic communication that is often discriminated against by neurotypical people.

Why do Autistic people tend to have blunt or direct communication
Autistic people need highly detailed communication.
Without this information we often find it difficult to communicate.
This means that often we are seen is blunt or rude, when what we need is direct and detailed communication.
Ongoing research by Rachel Cullen is exploring an “Autistic language hypothesis” that suggests Autistic people use and process language differently.

How to support a neurodivergent co-worker
Don’t invalidate
Believe them about their experience
Avoid unnecessary demands
Provide sensory breaks
Curate sensory environment
Know your obligations under the Equality Act 2010
Be prepared to source independent advocacy

Falling Through the Gap
An Autistic Drug Addict's Journey Through Recovery

BEFORE WE START
A note on this talk
This talk includes direct references to drug use, overdose, hospital admission, and the failures of mental health and substance use services. Nothing is included for shock value. Step out and back in as you need to.

INTRODUCTION
Founder, NeuroHub Community Ltd. Multiply neurodivergent practitioner, researcher, and writer. Ten years in recovery from drug addiction.
(Speaker notes: Brief. The point isn't the CV, it's establishing that the person describing the ecosystemic model today is the same person the model failed for a decade.)

THE FRAME
The ecosystemic model
Bodymind
The Autistic body and mind as one inseparable system, not a mind housed in a malfunctioning body.
→
Immediate Environment
Family, school, services, peer groups, the spaces a person actually has to survive inside day to day.
→
Power Structures
The institutions, policies and diagnostic systems that shape what the immediate environment is allowed to offer.
(Speaker notes: This is the theoretical spine of the whole talk. Distress is not manufactured inside the Autistic Bodymind, it is produced in the interaction between that Bodymind and the environments around it.)

Before the Drugs

BEFORE THE DRUGS
Growing up unseen
No diagnosis.
Just a child who didn't fit, in classrooms and friendship groups built for a different kind of nervous system.

BEFORE THE DRUGS
The psychosis nobody saw

posts.title: Falling through the gap: autism and addiction services: BEFORE THE DRUGS
posts.deck: Falling through the gap: autism and addiction services
posts.text:
BEFORE THE DRUGS
First contact
Drugs found what services never addressed.
It was relief.
(Speaker notes: This is the direct line from undiagnosed psychosis to first use: self-medication, not recreation. Frame it through the model: an Immediate Environment (services, family, school) that had not identified the condition left the Bodymind to solve the problem alone, and it found a solution.)

Community and Identity

COMMUNITY AND IDENTITY
Not shyness, not a preference for solitude.

COMMUNITY AND IDENTITY
Finding a tribe
(Speaker notes: This is one of the hardest things for professional audiences to sit with, that a substance-using community met needs that clinical services never touched. Say it without apologising for it.)

COMMUNITY AND IDENTITY
Identity, not just substance
Ecosystemically speaking: an Immediate Environment finally offered belonging that mainstream social spaces had withheld for years.

The Sensory Logic of Use

THE SENSORY LOGIC OF USE
Interoception, briefly
Interoception is the sense of what's happening inside your own body. Many Autistic people experience it differently: sometimes muted, sometimes overwhelming, rarely straightforward.

THE SENSORY LOGIC OF USE
Getting high as a stim
(Speaker notes: This reframes addiction as sensory regulation rather than escapism or hedonism. It's a genuinely useful clinical reframe for the room: ask what a person is regulating before assuming what they're avoiding.)

PSYCHONAUT
The psychonaut community
A subculture built around deliberate, documented exploration of psychoactive experience.

posts.title: Falling through the gap: autism and addiction services: PSYCHONAUT
posts.deck: Falling through the gap: autism and addiction services
posts.text:
PSYCHONAUT
Substance, quantity, combination, timing. Effects logged in detail, tracked over months and years. Not chaos. A methodology.

PSYCHONAUT
Pushing the edges
Curiosity and dysregulation were not two separate things happening at once.
They were the same process, wearing two names.
(Speaker notes: Resist a clean split between this was just an illness and this was just curiosity. Both were true simultaneously, and pretending otherwise flattens the experience.)

Falling Through the Gap

FALLING THROUGH THE GAP
Two doors, same answer
Mental Health Services
“We can't support you while you're using.”
Substance Use Services
“We can't help until your mental health is addressed.”

FALLING THROUGH THE GAP
The gap between two doors
Two services, two conditions, one person, and no door that opened.
It's what happens when Power Structures design services around single, separable diagnoses and hand the cost of that design to the person who doesn't fit it.
(Speaker notes: This is the Power Structures layer of the model made concrete: dual-diagnosis exclusion criteria as structural, not incidental, failure.)

THE NUMBERS
60+
hospital admissions in a single year
That's more than one a week. Every admission treated the overdose. None of them treated what caused it.
(Speaker notes: Let the number land without rushing past it. Follow with the observation that this is a system operating exactly as it was built to, repeatedly stabilising a crisis it was never designed to prevent.)

What Was Offered, and What Didn't Fit

posts.title: Falling through the gap: autism and addiction services: WHAT DIDN'T FIT
posts.deck: Falling through the gap: autism and addiction services
posts.text:
WHAT DIDN'T FIT
CBT
Offered repeatedly, as it is to many Autistic people. It asks you to restructure your thinking about a distress that was never generated by faulty thoughts.

WHAT DIDN'T FIT
Twelve-step programmes
Also offered repeatedly. Group-based, socially demanding, often spiritually or religiously framed, built around a model of surrender that assumes a shared social and cognitive style.
(Speaker notes: Name this as a documented pattern across the Autistic community, not just a personal gripe, monotropism and the double empathy problem are relevant background here if questions come up afterward.)

Bodymind
Addressed directly: the sensory and psychiatric needs drug use had been managing all along.
→
Immediate Environment
Rebuilt deliberately: relationships and routines that offered belonging without requiring use.
→
Power Structures
(Speaker notes: This is the ecosystemic model applied as a personal recovery methodology, not just a diagnostic lens. Be concrete about what changed in each of the three layers if time allows.)

CLOSING
What this means for practitioners
Stop asking which condition to treat first.
Start asking what the Bodymind is regulating, what the environment is withholding, and what the system is designed to exclude.
Meet the unmet needs and substance use will begin to stabilize,

posts.title: neurodiversity 101 language: Neurodiversity 101: The language of neurodiversity
posts.text:
Neurodiversity 101: The language of neurodiversity

Trigger Warning
This presentation contains discussion of words and symbols that may be triggering

What will we cover?
What is neurodiversity?
What is neurodivergent?
What is the pathology paradigm?
What is the neurodiversity paradigm?
Person-first vs identity-first language
Functioning Labels
Levels 1, 2, and 3
Aspergers
Puzzle Piece Symbols
Ableist Slurs

What is neurodiversity?
Neurodiversity refers to the biological diversity of brains in human society
No two brains are exactly the same
An individual can’t be neurodiverse, diversity requires a group of people with differences
Individuals can be neurodivergent

What is neurodivergent?
Neurodivergent means that a person diverges from what is considered normal or typical (neurotypical).
It refers to a wide array of neurocognitive styles
Often, Autistic and ADHD people will refer to themselves as neurodivergent
Mental health conditions, traumatic brain injury, and epilepsy are also examples of neurodivergence

What is the pathology paradigm?
The pathology paradigm is an overarching school of thought that views human difference through the lens of pathology.
Instead of calling someone Autistic they would say they have “Autism Spectrum Disorder”
Anyone that can not perform neurotypicality is viewed as disordered or having a condition requiring correction
Medical language surrounding neurodivergence is based on this paradigm

posts.title: neurodiversity 101 language: What is the neurodiversity paradigm?
posts.text:
What is the neurodiversity paradigm?
The neurodiversity paradigm see’s human diversity as a natural occurrence that is not in need of correction
It asks society to make space for us rather than correct us
The neurodiversity paradigm rejects words like “disorder” and “condition”
The neurodiversity paradigm rejects “cures” and “treatments” for Autistic experience

Person-first vs Identity-first Language
Person-First Language- “Person with Autism”
Identity-First Language- “Autistic Person”
Identity-Only Language- “Autie”
Out of 2,750 people surveyed, Autistic people vastly preferred Identity-First or Identity-Only
We do not need to be reminded we are a person
Being Autistic is a defining factor in our experience and interaction in the world

Functioning Labels
“High Functioning”- referring to people perceived to have less support needs
“Low Functioning”- referring to people perceived have significant support needs
Survey respondents vastly rejected functioning labels
They do not account for dynamic needs that change
They mislead about the amount of support or autonomy a person needs or has
They are intimately linked to the pathology paradigm

Levels 1, 2, and 3
New system that replaced functioning labels
Level 1 requires least support, Level 3 the most
Surveyed Autistic people by and large do not use levels
Similar arguments have been made about levels as with functioning labels

posts.title: neurodiversity 101 language: Aspergers
posts.text:
Aspergers
Removed as a diagnosis in 2013
Named after a member of the nazi party who performed eugenics on Autistic people
Often used as a covert functioning label
Surveyed community members widely reject the use of this label due to the reasons above

Puzzle Piece Symbols
The Puzzle Piece is largely rejected by the Autistic community
It’s use originated with the creation of the National Autistic Society who used an image of a puzzle piece with a male child crying as their logo
It has since gone on to be associated with many eugenics projects and the notorious Autism Speaks organisation that have done great harm to the community
Some Autistic people also suggest that it makes them feel like they are an incomplete puzzle

Ableist slurs
Unlike other minority groups, the Autistic community has not tried to reclaim the slurs used against it
For this reason words like r*tard and sp*stic are unanimously rejected within our community
It is felt that reclaiming these words would normalise their use by people who mean us harm.

posts.title: psychosis and alexithymia: Alexithymia & Psychosis In Autistic People
posts.text:
Alexithymia & Psychosis In Autistic People

Autistic, ADHD, Schizophrenic, Almost 10 Years Sober
Academic Researcher In Autistic Mental Health
Multiply Published Author
Neurodivergent Competent Mindfulness Practitioner
Student Member Of Complimentary Medical Association
Practitioner Member Of Addiction Professionals
Professional Member Of International Society Of Substance Use Professionals
Co-Founder Of Autistic Substance Use Network
Expert Advisor To International Coalition Against Restraint And Seclusion
Shortlisted Nominee In National Diversity Award 2025

Introduction
Why Does This Topic Matter?
Alexithymia is incredibly common in Autistic Populations.
Can be a factor in how Autistic people experience psychosis
What Is Alexithymia
Alexithymia is the inability to feel or articulate the emotions you are experiencing.
There are a number of explanations suggested for why this happens.

Introduction
What Is Psychosis
Psychosis is a state where perception, thinking, or beliefs become disconnected from our shared reality.
What is Alexithymia?
Alexithymia and Psychosis are common experiences for Autistic people but rarely discussed together.

Alexithymia In Autism
Notable Information About Alexithymia
Around 50–60% of Autistic people experience significant alexithymia
Not “lack of emotions”;  rather, difficulty mapping bodily sensations and internal states onto words
Often mistaken for “empathy deficits” or “flat affect”
Links to challenges with interoception (bodymind awareness of inner states)
Can complicate communication, relationships, and self-advocacy

posts.title: psychosis and alexithymia: Psychosis In Autism
posts.text:
Psychosis In Autism
Notable Information About Psychosis
Autistic people are at higher risk of psychosis than the general population
Psychosis in Autistic people is often misdiagnosed or overlooked due to diagnostic overshadowing
Experiences may include:
Voices or other perceptual changes
Paranoia or altered beliefs
Shifts in meaning-making and sense of self
Can be terrifying but also sometimes meaningful

How Alexithymia & Psychosis Interact
Alexithymia can make it harder to recognise early warning signs of psychosis
Emotional overwhelm may be felt as purely physical symptoms (racing heart, tension)
Difficulty articulating internal states causes delayed access to support
Misinterpretations by professionals (“non-compliance” or “lack of insight”)

This created a feedback loop: unrecognised distress → psychosis → increased distress

Professional & Systemic Issues
Psychiatry often frames both alexithymia and psychosis as “deficits” or “malfunctions”
Autistic ways of experiencing emotions and reality are pathologised
Lack of neurodivergent-competent approaches means Autistic voices are silenced
Services (like CAMHS, adult mental health, and substance-use services) often fail to adapt to Autistic needs

posts.title: psychosis and alexithymia: Rethinking Through Neurodivergent-Conpetence
posts.text:
Rethinking Through Neurodivergent-Conpetence
Alexithymia is not “broken empathy”; it’s a different way of relating to emotion
Psychosis is not always “meaningless madness”; it can communicate unmet needs or unprocessed trauma
Need to frame both within the neurodiversity paradigm:
Alexithymia = difference in interoceptive-emotional translation
Psychosis = altered states of meaning-making
Both can be understood as part of Autistic bodymind diversity

Rethinking Through Neurodivergent-Conpetence
Alexithymia is not “broken empathy”; it’s a different way of relating to emotion
Psychosis is not always “meaningless madness”; it can communicate unmet needs or unprocessed trauma
Need to frame both within the neurodiversity paradigm:
Alexithymia = difference in interoceptive-emotional translation
Psychosis = altered states of meaning-making
Both can be understood as part of Autistic bodymind diversity

Practical Strategies
For Autistic people experiencing both:
Develop body awareness practices (mindfulness, sensory check-ins)
Use external supports (mood charts, trusted others helping interpret states)
Recognise and honour psychotic experiences as valid expressions of self
For professionals:
Ask, don’t assume
Prioritise lived experience voices
Move beyond deficit-based models

Conclusion
Alexithymia and psychosis in Autistic people are deeply connected but under-researched
Both highlight the importance of neurodivergent-competent approaches
Final takeaway: We need to listen differently, support differently, and value Autistic meaning-making.
